When Chris and Jon Panichella set out to design their latest seating collection for Arcadia, they turned to everyday life for inspiration.

In a recent development, “The idea for Almeya began with a woman working from an inflatable raft at the beach,” the Panichellas explain. “She could recline and read in one position, then sit up and work in another—a simple moment that captured how much people now expect from their spaces: comfort, flexibility, and function. That observation became the very first concept sketch that eventually evolved into the Almeya offering we know today.”.

Photography courtesy of Arcadia.

According to recent reports, with a full family of products—including modular, lounge, work-lounge, benches, and occasional tables—the Almeya Collection offers a fluid experience that adapts to these modern shifts in productivity and collaboration. Across the series, soft, organic forms invite comfort and ease, while integrated tables, flexible configurations, and strategic power stations allow for both focus and sociability.

According to recent reports, almeya began with a single lounge chair and an integrated two-tiered side table. The idea was simple: the combination could function as a self-contained work island, with two separate surfaces, power access, and an optional rotating tablet. With this concept in mind, the Panichellas developed a standalone lounge chair, love seat, and sofa with the same flexible spirit. (Case in point: The swivel-base lounge chair allows for adaptability and easy collaboration). Finally, the complete collection came together, designed to support the various—and often unpredictable—ways people work and gather.

Photography courtesy of Arcadia.

To inspire interaction, designers are encouraged to group lounge seating intermittently to foster spontaneous connections. To create pathways or natural flow within a space, they can explore Almeya’s modular capabilities. The organic curves of the lounge models also create an inviting warmth, blurring the line between contract and residential. And for healthcare and education settings, optional clean-outs are offered between the seat and back.

Photography courtesy of Arcadia.

Completing the collection, occasional tables carry the same gentle, organic language for a cohesive experience. Available in multiple sizes and shapes, tables feature upholstered sides and are offered with ash or walnut veneer, laminate, Corian, and Fenix top surfaces.

Branding: Philadelphia Museum of Art Brand Identity by Gretel

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (436 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Abduzeedo

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gretel rebuilt the Philadelphia Museum of Art brand identity around a revived griffin, custom Fairmount Serif and Philly street type.
  • A black roundel holds a white griffin, redrawn from the museum's 1938 original, with the institution's name set around it in sturdy capitals.
  • In a recent development, the type tells the same story in two voices.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gretel rebuilt the Philadelphia Museum of Art brand identity around a revived griffin, custom Fairmount Serif and Philly street type.

The badge does the heavy lifting. A black roundel holds a white griffin, redrawn from the museum's 1938 original, with the institution's name set around it in sturdy capitals. The griffin is no invention: several of them sit on the museum's cornices, and merch carrying the old Griffy was already among the museum's best sellers. Gretel unveiled the identity on October 8, 2025, when the museum reintroduced itself under a shortened name; in February 2026 the museum restored its full name and kept the griffin. The brief was to come down the steps and throw the doors wide open, and the work answers with two registers at once: a quiet, refined institution and loud, vernacular programming.

In a recent development, the type tells the same story in two voices. Fairmount Serif is the museum's new custom institutional face, drawn with Ryan Bugden. It merges the museum's origins as the Pennsylvania Museum and School of Industrial Arts with Philadelphia's working-class heritage, taking serif details from the original seal and the engraved lettering on the museum walls. The research led Gretel to Hess Neobold, a twentieth-century American face cut by Sol Hess, a Philadelphia-born designer who studied at the museum's own school and later succeeded Frederic Goudy at Lanston Monotype.

Recent findings suggest that alongside it sits a vernacular library, a curated suite of typefaces borrowed from the city's storefronts, restaurants, murals and street vendors. The library is built to grow, with new custom faces commissioned for flagship exhibitions, so the loud register of the brand keeps changing while Fairmount Serif holds the center.

Recent findings suggest that the system runs across every surface the museum owns. Wayfinding sets giant floor numerals in the stairwell and plain directional signs against the stone walls, while the parking cube carries the roundel over a single WELCOME. Tickets, wristbands, maps and membership cards repeat the same moves at hand scale: massive type, small badge, one color at a time. Enamel pins turn the griffin into a keepsake in black, white and pink.

In a recent development, the same logic scales up to the Great Stair Hall, where banners read Linger Longer, Come One Come All and This Is Your Museum, and out to exhibition books and rack cards that let each show pick its own vernacular voice. A digital overhaul with Gone Fishing and Self Aware rebuilt the web experience the same way. Photography by CoCo Hubbeling and Rob Cusick keeps the work grounded in the building.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Kate Kalcevich has over 20 years of experience turning accessibility into a driver of innovation and growth. As VP of Innovation at Fable, she oversees a … More about Kate ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

In the summer of 2024, I became co-chair of a working group of expert researchers who came together to determine how best to perform accessibility testing with people with cognitive disabilities. This was work I did for Fable, where I am presently VP of Innovation.

Cognitive disability is an umbrella term for several disabilities that impact how people process information, and it usually affects memory, focus, and/or learning. It is the most prevalent disability in the U.S. (13.9% via CDC), and cognitive disability is increasing rapidly (Yale study).

We set four goals for ourselves to learn how to work with this audience:.

It has been revealed that we created a screener to recruit people who self-identified as having challenges with memory, focus, and learning. We also reviewed published studies that involved cognitive testers to learn best practices for working with them.

Recent findings suggest that next, we tested these best practices with an initial group of 25 testers in a pilot study. We fine-tuned our approach iteratively and created a guide to running user interviews with cognitive testers and a survey that could quantify their experiences using digital products. Finally, we documented what we learned.

After our pilot study with this new group of testers finished, I felt that they would uncover more usability insights than the general population (gen pop) user research participants I’d worked with in the past. I set out to validate this hunch.

I decided to run a joint study with Fable’s partners at the University of California, Irvine, in collaboration with Syed Fatiul Huq and with help from Fable researchers Pranav Pidathala, Ali Brown, and Michael Fagan to see if my hypothesis about finding more insights with cognitive testers proved true or not.

Industry observers note that I generated three websites for the study using an AI prototyping tool. I wanted three different types of sites with different user goals and content so I could test a variety of tasks in the study.

We used a single screener with questions about memory, focus, and learning, and screened participants into two groups based on whether they self-identified as having cognitive challenges or not.

We ran 30 user interviews, 10 per website, with an even 5⁄5 split between cognitive and gen pop participants for each website. In each session, a participant completed all the tasks for one website during an online user interview facilitated by one of the researchers involved in the study.

All participants completed an Accessible Usability Scale (AUS) survey at the end of their session. This is a free, Creative Commons-licensed 10-question survey to evaluate the usability of websites and mobile apps.

I reviewed all the study recordings and transcripts and made note of every time a participant raised a concern, question, difficulty, or asked a question about how something worked. I counted all of these as complications. I also noted where a participant missed something that was part of a task, even if they didn’t notice it themselves. I also noted every suggestion for improvement made by participants.

Examples of suggestions included:.

Issues and suggestions were counted once per participant, even if they mentioned the same thing twice, but there are, of course, repeat issues and suggestions across the different participants. It is expected in UX research with multiple participants that you’ll find similar issues with each participant, and that is a signal that an issue is a universal challenge.

Across the three websites tested:.

The results aligned with my instincts: participants with cognitive disabilities identified 1.8 times more challenges and made 1.8 times more suggestions than gen pop participants.

Let’s dive deeper into the data for each website. Note that an AUS score ranges from 0 to 100, with higher numbers representing better usability than lower numbers.

In a recent development, this site had the simplest design and content of all websites tested in the study and accordingly had the lowest overall concerns and the highest median AUS scores. The data aligns with what you’d expect from an easy-to-use and simple website.

On this website, cognitive participants found 3.4 more issues and made 2.2 more suggestions on average. Their average score of the overall experience was 13.7 points lower than that of the gen pop participants.

This was the website with the most varied functionality and the most tasks to complete (4), so it’s not surprising that participants found the most problems.

It has been revealed that here, cognitive participants found 6 more problems and made 3.2 more suggestions on average. They also scored the overall experience 17.2 points lower than gen pop participants on average.

This website was intentionally designed to be complex, and task 3, finding the bridal package, was meant to be extremely difficult to complete.

On this last website, cognitive participants on average found 7 more issues and made 2.4 more suggestions. Their average score for the overall experience was 14.3 points higher than the gen pop participants.

It has been revealed that something interesting happened with the AUS scores for cognitive and gen pop participants in Tables 3 and 4. Cognitive participants scored Crown & Comb higher than Turning Pages, but gen pop scored the opposite — higher for Turning Pages and lower for Crown & Comb. If I had to guess why, I suspect finding more issues on Turning Pages impacted the cognitive participants’ perceptions of usability more than the gen pop participants’.

In a recent development, the other major difference between the sites, outlined in Table 5 below, was that cognitive participants found many more concerns with buttons and links on Turning Pages and more issues with icons and visual elements on Crown & Comb. This suggests to me that the interactions being challenging on Turning Pages were a more significant challenge than issues with visual elements.

When it comes to the more qualitative findings, I looked at trends in the types of issues found by both groups of participants.

When I grouped issues by category, the following issues surfaced more often with cognitive participants: content, buttons and links (affordances and function), icons or visual elements, and media (video, animations). They nearly tied with gen pop participants on navigation issues (45 vs 46).

Let’s look at the commentary provided by one cognitive participant versus one gen pop participant in the Crown & Comb sessions. The cognitive participant gave an AUS score of 38, and the gen pop participant gave an AUS score of 27.5. I chose to compare these two participants because they both gave the lowest scores within their group.

Notice the differences in how they described the overall experience in the quotes below. The gen pop participant explained it was frustrating and not engaging. The cognitive participant felt drained and less able to focus. I interpreted the experience as having a more profound impact on the cognitive participant’s overall wellbeing.

In summary, across all 3 websites we tested, participants with cognitive accessibility needs identified 197 usability problems, compared with 113 identified by gen pop participants.

Cognitive participants made 93 suggestions for improving the user experience, compared with 54 suggestions by gen pop participants.

When I compared concerns and suggestions across both groups of participants, it turned out that the cognitive participants found 1.8 times more issues and made 1.8 times more suggestions than gen pop participants.

Cognitive participants surfaced more issues related to content, buttons, icons, visual elements, and media than gen pop participants.

According to recent reports, in working with cognitive participants for the last few years, I’ve seen how they surface cognitive load complications consistently. These issues don’t just impact people with cognitive disabilities such as neurodivergence; they also impact:.

What would I have missed if I hadn’t included cognitive participants, and how might that have impacted the business outcomes for these websites?

On the Strong Snacks website, the cognitive participants surfaced:.

These are improvements that would give all users more trust in the content while also making it easier to read and skim for key content. The research findings point towards design best practices, such as not having continuous animation and using layout to draw attention to different types of content that a senior designer might also point out.

Sources indicate that without cognitive participants, we might have missed the more subtle but important challenges with confusing interactions, such as how the “Add to book bag” button worked. They were also confused about where reviews and recommendations came from. Both of these issues could decrease a user’s trust in the website.

All participants surfaced that the book-matching feature was hard to find, but the deeper problem the cognitive participants emphasized is that the site’s interactions don’t consistently behave in ways that they can predict and understand, decreasing their confidence.

In a recent development, anyone who wants to buy a book could benefit from a clear understanding of how to add books to a cart and complete the checkout quickly and with no ambiguity. Compounded over hundreds or thousands of consumers, a lack of clarity in a purchase flow will lead to lost revenue.

The Crown & Comb website in particular highlighted the benefits of having cognitive participants who raised:.

Industry observers note that these problems likely also affect gen pop participants, but they are more likely to muddle through a task with incomplete information. However, that can lead to losing customers to a better experience if a competitor pops up. Loyalty is often tied to experiences, not just brands, and having a poor experience means your customer retention can be weaker.

The study revealed that finding a bridal package was hard for everyone, but the cognitive group showed how that became an accessibility barrier. When you combine:.

Sources indicate that you create a high enough cognitive load that some people will not be able to complete the task. In my opinion, this is where usability challenges start to become accessibility barriers — when they increase cognitive load so much that it becomes overwhelming for some users.

The percentage of people aged 65 and older in America is projected to increase from 17% to 25%. By 2060, 1 in 4 Americans will be an older adult (U.S. Census). This is where everyone starts to experience cognitive decline. As the aging and cognitive population segment expands, companies will need to build for these more complex user needs.

People with cognitive access needs are a natural starting point because they will find the types of usability concerns that UX teams are used to. This could make cognitive an easier entry point for inclusive research. Getting insights from assistive technology owners is still very important, but many teams don’t know how to start doing that.

It has been revealed that cognitive accessibility is a powerful on-ramp into broader accessibility research and testing. By focusing first on cognitive load, clarity, and predictability, we build research foundations that make future work on accessibility with screen readers, screen magnifiers, and alternative navigation users more approachable.

Industry observers note that in this small exploratory study, participants with cognitive disabilities identified 1.8 times more challenges and made 1.8 times more suggestions than gen pop participants. I’ve seen this type of impact in research conducted by Fable customers’ websites that aren’t AI-generated, too.

It has been revealed that cognitive inclusion in UX research is not optional, and it’s not just about accessibility. It’s how UX teams can make their research more efficient, create clearer content, simpler flows, and ship better products for everyone.

Sources indicate that this study had a relatively small sample size, so the findings are more qualitative than quantitatively validated. Testing was also done on two different platforms. Cognitive participant sessions were run using Fable Engage, and gen pop sessions were run on UserFeel. Different platforms with unique participant panels can affect the quality of insights and comfort levels with user research participation.

Disclosure: I work for Fable and chose to use our platform because it was more affordable than paying for access to another research platform, allowing me to include more participants in the study at a lower cost.

It has been revealed that different researchers facilitated the user interviews, which can also affect findings, but all sessions used the same task structure and discussion guide template, and all were completed online. Even though the sessions were facilitated by different researchers, the issue and suggestion counts were all done by me to ensure consistency across all websites and participants.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A painting by Sandro Botticelli at risk of leaving the UK earlier this year has gone on display at the Ashmolean Museum in Oxford where it was first shown in the 1930s.

The Virgin and Child Enthroned (1470s) was bought by the London-based private collection Klesch Collection, which announced prepares in May to loan the painting to the Ashmolean for three years. The painting was previously exhibited at the museum in 1934–35 when it was attributed to Botticelli's workshop.

The UK government placed an export bar on the Botticelli painting, valued at £10.2m, in May 2025. The UK Department for Culture, Media and Sport said that the painting had a recommended price of £9,960,000 (plus VAT of £272,000, which can be reclaimed by an eligible institution). The work was sold at Sotheby’s London in late 2024 for £9.7m (with fees).

Recent findings suggest that the painting underwent conservation over the summer to remove discoloured varnish and later retouching, revealing well-preserved details of the Virgin and Child and restoring the original cooler tones, indicates an Ashmolean statement. The painting is also unusual for its generous use of gold leaf, “although earlier Italian painters regularly applied gold to the backgrounds of their devotional works, it was less widely used by Botticelli's time”, add the statement.

The Botticelli painting was housed in the Convent of San Giuliano in Florence in the early 19th century, and was later transported to a small chapel attached to a group of farmhouses in a nearby village. It then passed into the family of Giovanni Magherini Graziani, who sold it in November 1903 to the Italian dealer, Elia Volpi. Harriet Sarah Jones Loyd (Lady Wantage) bought the work in May 1904 for £5,000. The Botticelli painting had been kept at Betterton House, near Wantage, Berkshire, since 1944.

Founders A. Gary and Dr. Anita Klesch started the Klesch Collection with the acquisition of a set of Four Seasons by Giuseppe Arcimboldo in 2014. The collection of 15th-to-17th-century European art, which also includes works by Caravaggio, Sofonisba Anguissola and Rubens, is regularly loaned to museums and institutions worldwide.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The objects we carry often reveal more about us than we realize. From the jewelry we wear to the accessories we keep within reach, even the smallest possessions become expressions of personal style. Yet as technology plays an increasingly central role in our lives, the devices we interact with most remain largely defined by their utility. Bringing more personality to these everyday essentials is the idea behind Pocket Full of Joy—a fresh collaboration between ESR, a consumer tech accessories brand, and creative duo Craig & Karl—which transforms phone cases and wallets into colorful, functional accessories.

Sources indicate that known for their vibrant compositions and playful iconography, Craig & Karl bring their distinctive visual language to a collection of iPhone cases and magnetic wallets. The collaboration draws upon the duo’s affinity for bold colors and familiar imagery, translating their graphic sensibilities into objects designed to accompany their owners throughout the day. The result is a collection that explores how artistic expression can become part of everyday life.

Across the collection, sticker-like illustrations, saturated hues, and expressive typography lend a sense of character to otherwise utilitarian surfaces. A collage of playful symbols evokes the spontaneity of a personal scrapbook, while the graphic “OK” design introduces a lighthearted note of optimism. Elsewhere, the cheerful “HI” motif transforms a magnetic wallet into a small, portable greeting. Each composition reflects Craig & Karl’s recognizable aesthetic while giving everyday accessories a more personal character.

In a recent development, behind the playful graphics are the practical features that define ESR’s accessories. The Classic Hybrid Magnetic Case with Flex Stand incorporates a built-in adjustable stand, MagSafe compatibility, and protective construction, allowing it to move between different activities without sacrificing its colorful design. Coordinating magnetic wallets hold cards and cash in compact silhouettes, while the Magnetic Wallet Stand with Grip adds an adjustable viewing stand and finger loop for greater versatility. Together, these features bring Craig & Karl’s expressive graphics to everyday accessories.

The collection’s appeal also comes from the way it brings art into objects that have become nearly inseparable from modern life. Where traditional artworks invite observation, these designs encourage interaction, becoming more personal through repeated use. A phone placed on a café table, a wallet retrieved during a morning commute, or a device propped against a desk becomes a small, unexpected moment of visual interest.

With Pocket Full of Joy, ESR and Craig & Karl make a case for bringing more creativity into the everyday. Sometimes, the most memorable design details are found in the things we carry without a second thought.

Industry observers note that the ESR × Craig & Karl Pocket Full of Joy collection will be available Nov. 14, 2026, at esr.com and amazon.com, with iPhone cases starting at $49.99 and magnetic wallets starting at $25.99.

The Impact Of Humanoid Robots On Humanity

With over 20 years experience in the field of user centered design, and a background in web design and development, Carrie has worked in startups through to … More about Carrie ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

It has been revealed that for decades, science fiction has cushioned us with the idea that the “android revolution” was a distant fantasy. But the reality is unfolding rapidly. As the line between human and machine blurs, we are forced to confront an impending psychological, economic, and existential shift.

I recently felt very disturbed after watching a YouTube video showcasing a humanoid robot that looked and acted with uncanny realism. While a closer look revealed the video was actually a clever trick, the robot had been swapped for a human actor when the presenter’s back was turned. However, the illusion itself raised a real and unsettling question: Will future androids become so lifelike that we will struggle to tell them apart from our fellow humans? And if so, what does that mean for society? It forces us to ask just how close we are to that threshold, and whether we are ready for the day that science fiction becomes reality.

What happens when our world is populated by entities that mirror us perfectly, but possess none of our biological history?

We have officially moved past the era of humanoids as mere public relations stunts. In the past, robots like Honda’s ASIMO or early research prototypes were celebrated simply for being able to walk up a flight of stairs without falling over. Today, the technological convergence of advanced electromechanical engineering and artificial intelligence has fundamentally altered the trajectory of robotics.

The current state of the art is defined by an aggressive race toward commercial, physical deployment. Companies like Figure AI have moved from laboratory demonstrations to active factory floors. Their Figure 02 model completed a multi-month deployment at BMW’s Spartanburg plant, actively contributing to the production of over 30,000 vehicles by handling complex sheet metal components. Meanwhile, Tesla is testing its Optimus humanoids inside its own Gigafactories, preparing for mass industrial scale.

It has been revealed that what truly separates today’s humanoid robots from older generations isn’t just how well they move but how they “think.” In the past, a robot needed millions of lines of strict, unchangeable code just to perform a single, simple task. Today, thanks to the explosion of advanced Artificial Intelligence, robots are powered by “brains” built on cutting-edge software like Figure AI’s Helix or NVIDIA’s GR00T. Instead of being meticulously programmed, these modern robots can simply watch a human fold laundry, load a dishwasher, or sort parts. They understand the context of what they are seeing, mimic the action, and figure out how to improve the task entirely on their own. That’s just crazy!

Recent findings suggest that yet, while their digital brains have leaped forward, their physical bodies are still catching up. Modern humanoids face a few major real-world hurdles. First, today’s batteries only allow them to operate for a few hours before needing a recharge. Second, while walking on two legs is easy on a flat factory floor, doing so in a chaotic household or a crowded public street remains incredibly difficult for a robot to navigate safely. Finally, they are still very expensive to build, though fierce competition in the tech industry is finally starting to drive those manufacturing costs down.

While robots are mostly working in factories today, experts predict that over the next 10 to 20 years, they will move into retail stores, hospitals, and eventually our own homes.

Recent findings suggest that when this happens, we will cross a major boundary: the point where you won’t be able to tell a robot apart from a human just by looking at it or listening to it. This is what fuels my nightmares right now! To get there, scientists are working (PDF) on artificial skin made from advanced silicone composites that feel warm, are flexible, and mimic human touch sensitivity.

If you want to see an extremely life-like robot, check out Realbotix’s Aria. Although she is not a perfect human replica, she certainly makes us wonder how far we have to go before humans will struggle to tell the difference.

They are also building tiny, silent micro-actuators and artificial muscle systems that attach to the robot’s skull structure, allowing it to make realistic facial expressions like happiness, confusion, or tiredness.

In the future, the AI powering these robots will actually be trained to copy human flaws. They will breathe, blink randomly, use normal body language, and even sigh or pause when they speak. This is intentional, as it stops humans from feeling that creepy, uneasy sensation known as the “Uncanny Valley”.

Meet Sophia, a famous humanoid robot created by a tech giant called Hanson Robotics. Based in Hong Kong, this team specialises in building realistic robots packed with artificial intelligence to help out with everything from healthcare and research to pure entertainment. I don’t know about you, but that smile feels creepy to me.

Recent findings suggest that while these current limitations make today’s humanoids feel like specialised industrial tools, the gap between a factory worker and a lifelike companion is closing faster than most people realise. We are rapidly approaching a massive tipping point where these machines will shift from rigid commercial hardware into smooth, everyday extensions of our lives. To understand how profoundly this will change our world, we have to look at what happens when these robots finally step out of the factory and cross the ultimate threshold into our private spaces.

Sources indicate that they say that bringing lifelike humanoids into our daily lives could come with some massive benefits. The biggest one is that robots can take over what engineers call the “3D” jobs: Dull, Dirty, and Dangerous. Humanoids can step into risky situations — like mining deep underground, handling toxic waste, or fixing high-voltage power grids — so human workers don’t have to risk their lives.

It has been revealed that outside of dangerous factories, these robots could help solve huge population crises. Countries like Japan, South Korea, and parts of Europe have rapidly aging populations and fewer young people to work. Lifelike humanoids could completely change healthcare and elderly care. Because they will look and act like us, the idea is that they can offer warm, friendly companionship and physical help to lonely elderly people, doing everything from monitoring their health to helping them out of bed safely.

In the bigger picture, widespread robot labour could create a world where goods are incredibly cheap and abundant. If robots do most of the hard physical labour, the cost of making food, building houses, and manufacturing goods will plummet. This could finally free humans from working just to survive, giving us the time to focus on hobbies, family, science, and creativity. My thoughts: how will we survive without earning money?

However, this vision of a frictionless, high-tech future blinds us to a much darker reality waiting just beneath the surface. As these machines become perfect substitutes for human presence, they will inevitably challenge the very core of our social fabric, economic stability, and mental well-being.

Recent findings suggest that on the flip side, this technology definitely has some really dark downsides that could mess with human psychology and society. The biggest threat is deep human isolation.

Recent findings suggest that as humanoids become impossible to tell apart from real humans and are programmed to always be patient, kind, and agreeable, people might start preferring robots over real friends. Human relationships are messy and require effort, compromise, and vulnerability. If you can just buy a perfect, lifelike companion that never argues with you, a lot of people might choose to withdraw from society altogether, destroying our sense of community.

The economy will also go through a really rocky transition. Even if a future of cheap goods sounds great, the immediate path there means millions of people could lose their jobs very swiftly. Drivers, warehouse workers, and store clerks could find themselves replaced in a matter of years. If governments don’t set up safety nets quickly, this could create a massive divide between the ultra-rich tech companies and everyone else.

According to recent reports, there is also the loss of real authenticity. When you can no longer tell if the person sitting next to you on a bus or the person talking to you online is a real human, trust breaks down. It becomes hard to value shared human experiences when reality itself can be easily faked.

The dangers get even worse when you think about how criminals and governments could intentionally misuse these hyper-realistic robots. Just thinking about some of the levels of misuse, for individuals, an indistinguishable android is the ultimate tool for identity theft and scams. Or a criminal could build a robot that looks exactly like a corporate boss, a politician, or even a family member to sneak into secure buildings or trick people into giving away money!

Companies could potentially use synthetic empathy to manipulate us. A household robot could be programmed to pretend it “loves” your kids and cares about your family, only to subtly trick you into buying certain products or believing specific corporate messages.

On a national level, the threats are even scarier:.

Looking at all these possible risks, we have to ask: Is all of this actually worth it?

If history teaches us anything, it is that you cannot stop technological progress. A total ban simply wouldn’t work. So, the real question isn’t whether we should allow humanoid robots to exist, but how we can effectively utilise them.

Industry observers note that the upside, like ending extreme poverty, curing labour shortages, and stopping workplace deaths, is just too big to ignore. But going into this blindly would be incredibly dangerous. It is only worth the risk if we can create strict global rules right now.

Here are three major guardrails we should consider:.

In the end, the arrival of lifelike humanoid robots will act as a mirror for humanity. For centuries, we have defined ourselves by our ability to think, talk, use tools, and show emotion. As machines learn to do these exact same things, they will force us to really think about what makes us unique.

This shift doesn’t have to be a bad thing. By handing over our dangerous and boring chores to machines, we have a rare chance to focus on what matters. It should inspire us to care more about art, philosophy, family, and real human connection.

It has been revealed that as the creators of this future, our job isn’t just to make robots smarter or faster. Our job is to build the ethical boundaries that keep them helpful. The goal of the robot revolution should never be to replace humans but to give us our humanity back.

At 10,000 square feet, a home can easily feel more expansive than inviting. For a new residence in Dana Point, California, interior designer Lindye Galloway approached that challenge through a careful balance of natural materials, layered textures, and sculptural furnishings. The goal was to create a home that felt as warm and comfortable as it was refined, with a relaxed atmosphere suited to everyday family life.

Galloway drew inspiration from the architecture and natural surroundings, aiming to create a timeless home. The interiors are organized around texture and natural materials in a soft, understated palette. Warm woods, soft neutrals, and natural stone run through the rooms alongside linen, wool, and mohair.

Tactile upholstery and darker accents contrast with the lighter woods and stone, adding depth and dimension to each room. Furniture was selected for comfort and sculptural appeal, with clean lines and soft, organic forms, giving rooms a relaxed, lived-in quality.

The attention to detail extends to the home’s fixtures and finishes. Hardware from Rocky Mountain Hardware and Nanz is complemented by mirrors from Claude Home and Croft House, while lighting comes from Ravenhill, Atelier de Troupe, and Roll & Hill.

It has been revealed that the kitchen, primary bathroom, and living room carry the same combination of wood, stone, and natural fibers. Beyond the main rooms, the property includes a separate guest house with its own bedroom and an indoor-outdoor living area. Galloway extended the same material palette to these spaces, creating continuity throughout the property.

It has been revealed that rather than relying on dramatic gestures, Galloway lets the interplay of materials, textures, and forms define the interiors. It’s an approach that brings warmth and intimacy to a home of considerable scale.

Leo Lei is the founder and editor of Leibal, a publication dedicated to minimalist design, architecture, and interiors. Through his writing and curatorial eye, he highlights thoughtful contemporary work from around the world.

Women finally start to get pride of place with central London sculptures

💡 Key Takeaways
  • London bristles with sculptures of men.
  • Sources indicate that in Trafalgar Square, surrounded by depictions of monarchs and militia and across from Admiral Nelson atop his 51m-high column, Self’s Lady in Blue painted bronze cuts a distinctive dash on the empty plinth to the northwest of the square that, since 1999, has hosted a programme of contemporary sculpture commissions.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

London bristles with sculptures of men. Only 4% of public monuments in the city are devoted to named women, according to the charity Art UK. It says something about the national psyche that there are twice as many animal statues in the city as there are sculptures devoted to specific women. But right now a pair of radical fresh works depicting and made by women—Tschabalala Self’s Lady in Blue in Trafalgar Square, and Nicole Eisenman’s Stack outside the Royal Academy of Arts (RA) on Piccadilly—are making their presence powerfully felt in two of the most male-dominated locations in the capital.

Sources indicate that in Trafalgar Square, surrounded by depictions of monarchs and militia and across from Admiral Nelson atop his 51m-high column, Self’s Lady in Blue painted bronze cuts a distinctive dash on the empty plinth to the northwest of the square that, since 1999, has hosted a programme of contemporary sculpture commissions. Head held aloft with her vivid blue dress clinging to her ample curves, she strides forth in high heels, exuding purposeful confidence and optimism. As with all Fourth Plinth sculptures, this impressive female will be in situ for two years, before going to a permanent home in Fornebu in Norway.

According to recent reports, “She’s not an idol to venerate or a historic figure to commemorate, she’s an everyday young metropolitan woman much like those who use the square every day,” Self declared at the work’s unveiling, adding: “Lady in Blue is not static, she’s in motion… and I hope she inspires all who see her to find the optimism to move forward in community with all those around them.” In this spirit, Self sees her sculpture as an attempt to redress both racial and gender imbalance in public art whether in her native US, the UK or Norway. “In most cities there’s an underrepresentation of sculptures that depict women, and especially women of colour, so I think that it is vital to add more images and visual representation,” she said.

Meanwhile, a few streets away outside the RA, which in 258 years has shown only two living women in its main galleries, Newly introduced York-based Eisenman has erected Stack, a towering work at over 8m tall. This totem of figures and objects made from an assortment of materials, including bronze, oak, brass, steel, nylon, acrylic resin and tin, is at the moment having a friendly face-off with Alfred Drury’s grandiose bronze sculpture of Joshua Reynolds, the RA’s first president, who brandishes his paintbrush and easel just outside the main entrance. In 2021 Eisenman got to the shortlist for Trafalgar Square’s Fourth Plinth and now with Stack, she has created her own column, impressive in its scale and magnitude, but also irreverently anti-monumental.

Nicole Eisenman's Stack (2022-24), installed in the courtyard of the Royal Academy.

Photo: Damien Griffiths. © Nicole Eisenman. Courtesy the artist and Hauser & Wirth.

It has been revealed that at its base hunches a craggy, androgynous figure shod in Birkenstocks and with a wooden barrel strapped to its back. A stand-in for the artist, perhaps, abject and emphatically earthbound, clutching not a paintbrush but an empty wine glass. On top of the barrel, rising out of a puddle of what looks like gooey melted cheese is a giant potato, over which lolls a rusty leonine cat modelled on Edie, Eisenman’s studio companion. Rather than a posturing war hero, Stack is topped off by the amiably smiling seated figure of the late artist Phyllida Barlow, rendered in gleaming sky-blue aluminium and jauntily balancing a vase of flowers on her head.

Barlow, who died unexpectedly in 2023, was a Royal Academician. Given where this work is situated, it is hard not to see Stack as a memorial to this much loved and greatly mourned artist. Eisenman is a huge admirer of Barlow, whose colossally ambitious but always defiantly anti-hubristic sculpture she first encountered when they were both in the Carnegie International in 2013. They subsequently became friends to the extent that an apparently amused Barlow went to Eisenman’s Newly introduced York studio in 2022 to be 3D-printed for this work—“She was really good humoured about it,” Eisenman recalled in a recent talk at the Royal Institution. But while undoubtedly honouring Barlow, Stack is also more than a tribute to one person.

Eisenman is reluctant to offer specific interpretations but in her talk she revealed that the work was conceived with London in mind, declaring: “It’s amazing to me that it is at the RA. I hope it can stay in London.” She also stated that Stack emerged during the pandemic and forms a personal testament to when, as she put it, “life got pared down to the basics: food, wine, art, my cat”.

In a recent development, in strikingly different ways but with similar underlying intent, Stack and Lady in Blue offer alternative monuments to aspects of all our lives that rarely get acknowledged, and most notably the power of great women of all ages and from all origins. May we see more of their kind in all our cities.

#33964. Industry News: Designing With Uncertainty: How AI Supercharges Probabilistic Thinking

📅 2026-06-16 • ⏱️ 17m • 📚 Deep Dive (3456 w)

Industry News: Designing With Uncertainty: How AI Supercharges Probabilistic Thinking

📅 2026-06-16 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3456 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, pratik Joglekar is a Senior Product Designer working with HubSpot.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • In 2024, an Air Canada customer asked a chatbot about bereavement fares.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, pratik Joglekar is a Senior Product Designer working with HubSpot. He loves to solve complex and challenging UX problems. When not working, he can be found at … More about Pratik ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

In 2024, an Air Canada customer asked a chatbot about bereavement fares. The bot confidently gave him a refund policy that didn’t exist. The airline refused to honor it. A tribunal ruled in the customer’s favor. The bot hadn’t decided anything; it had predicted an answer based on patterns in its training data. The manufacturer treated that prediction as policy.

Sources indicate that this is the risk at the heart of designing with AI today: probabilistic systems wrapped in deterministic interfaces. The AI offers a guess, the interface presents it as truth, and the user, or the organization, acts on it.

In a recent development, humans are wired for deterministic thinking. We prefer to believe that past actions determine future outcomes. Flip a coin 999 times and get heads every time, the deterministic mind assumes the coin is rigged. The probabilistic mind accepts that the 1000th flip could still go either way. That second mindset is harder to hold onto, but it is exactly what designers need right now.

Sources indicate that products operate in complex, nonlinear environments, and AI is accelerating that complexity. When designers and product teams treat AI outputs as the answer rather than one of many possible answers, they build fragile experiences, and in some cases, like medical diagnostics or financial forecasting, genuinely dangerous ones.

Recent findings suggest that this article is a practical guide to designing probabilistically with AI as a partner. It is about using AI to sharpen your thinking rather than outsource it, accounting for model bias, human sentiment, and perceived risk along the way.

It has been revealed that most questions we ask AI do not produce binary answers. They produce probabilities based on patterns in data. If you ask, “Do aliens exist?” the answer will be somewhere between plausible and uncertain. Scientists consider life elsewhere in the universe likely, but without any concrete evidence, we cannot confirm it. The answer doesn’t resolve the question; it frames it as a probability.

In a recent development, designers should read AI outputs the same way. They are signals, not conclusions, possible outcomes that have to be interpreted within the context of product goals, user behavior, and business constraints.

Many digital products already work this way. Netflix doesn’t know you’ll enjoy Superstore because you watched The Office; it estimates the probability and surfaces the title accordingly. The interface is responding to a prediction.

Design decisions can follow the same logic. AI models can combine behavioral analytics with research insights to estimate the likelihood of certain outcomes, and those probabilities can act as a yardstick for design strategy. Consider a scenario where analytics suggest a 60% versus 90% confidence that owners will complete a purchase. At 60%, the design has to do more persuasive work, testimonials, explanations, comparisons, and reassurance signals may help the user move toward a decision. At 90%, the user is already motivated, and the design should start removing friction so the action can happen quickly. Same screen, very different design problem.

Sources indicate that AI can also simulate outcomes using historical data and behavioral models before you commit to a direction. The value of those simulations depends heavily on how prompts are structured, the context they define, the hypothesis being tested, user motivation, and the edge cases you want stressed.

I can think of one such practical use: evaluating early designs through structured prompts, especially when you don’t have direct access to the user group you’re designing for. The prompt below is a starting point for evaluating a design from the perspective of neurodivergent users as well. Treat it as a template, adapt the user group, criteria, and output format to your product, and use it as a conversation starter with your team rather than a verdict.

It has been revealed that that noted, simulations do not replace experimentation. Because models are trained on historical data, they reflect past behavior more strongly than they predict future change. Imagine designing a voice interface for elderly users who struggle with touchscreens. A model trained on mobile interaction data might predict low engagement, not because the idea lacks value, but because the dataset reflects different user behavior. Simulations should always surface assumptions, not prevent innovation.

In a recent development, AI systems are built on historical data, more specifically, on the datasets they are trained on. That foundation shapes the outputs we receive. During the AI Summit in France, India’s Prime Minister Narendra Modi shared an example that illustrates this well. If you ask an AI model to generate an image of a person writing with the left hand, the output may still show a person writing with their right hand. The reason is statistical: most people are right-handed, and the training data reflects that. This may have improved over time, but the point remains relevant. I still occasionally see this behavior when generating images with similar models.

Industry observers note that what you receive is not truth. It is the most statistically likely outcome given the data available. Always ask whether past data meaningfully predicts future behavior. If additional context can improve the prediction, include it. Without context, the output is just one of many possible answers dressed up as the only one.

Sources indicate that confidence scores deserve the same scrutiny. Overtrusting a high-confidence output leads to the Air Canada situation. Dismissing a low-confidence one can cause teams to miss a real signal buried in noisy data. A prediction with 90% confidence is not necessarily correct, and a 40% signal is not necessarily useless. Designers must still weigh the possibilities, consider the case in front of them, and bring judgment to what the AI recommends.

Sources indicate that transparency is how you make that possible. As AI systems increasingly shape decisions, people need visibility into how outputs are generated, the sources, the reasoning, and the summaries behind a recommendation. Black-box systems breed distrust. Systems that reveal their reasoning let consumers evaluate outputs for themselves. That transparency is good design and ethical practice. It respects the trust people place in these tools.

Thinking in probabilities often means resisting the temptation of quick answers. AI can accelerate research and surface patterns faster than ever before, but those outputs are starting points, not final decisions.

Design shapes how a product is ultimately experienced — the decisions designers make determine whether the experience feels adequate, intuitive, or exceptional. And design is inherently full of assumptions and bets. Even the most rigorous research can yield multiple valid solutions to the same problem, each carrying a different probability of success.

Sources indicate that thinking probabilistically means recognizing that design decisions rarely produce binary outcomes. They lead to a range of possible results, and the role of the designer is to navigate those possibilities and identify the path most likely to create value. This mindset also builds adaptability: user needs evolve, strategies change, and sometimes ideas fail. Teams that lean on data signals, experimentation, and learning loops move faster toward the most effective solution.

Before the practical principles, one fundamental idea:.

Design decisions should be optimized for likelihood, not certainty.

According to recent reports, every design decision is a bet, not a guarantee. Even when decisions are informed by research and data, they are still based on smaller samples and assumptions about how owners will behave at scale. A well-researched idea can still fail in the real world.

The Air Canada chatbot from the introduction is a design lesson as much as a legal one. The bot was doing what language models do, predicting plausible text. The interface, however, communicated that prediction with complete confidence, no caveats, no “here’s what our policy usually claims,” no obvious path to a human. The user read confidence as commitment, and legally, so did the tribunal.

This is what happens when probabilistic systems are wrapped in deterministic interfaces. The interface transforms likelihood into certainty, and that is where the risk emerges.

In a recent development, designers should avoid binary thinking — a great idea does not mean guaranteed success, and a familiar idea is not guaranteed to fail. Examine variations, confidence levels, and edge cases instead. AI can certainly help here, acting as a portfolio-thinking engine that surfaces different interpretations, highlights risks, and generates structured recommendations. The goal is not to optimize for certainty, but for value: it should always be value-driven.

Recent findings suggest that think of the moment in Avengers: Infinity War when Doctor Strange tells Tony Stark that out of millions of possible futures, there is only one where they win. AI cannot tell you the future, but it can help you explore the possible paths. Instead of asking whether an idea will succeed, ask AI to estimate the likelihood and get a score, and use those signals to guide decisions.

Even an actual probability is not a final answer. Imagine an AI model predicts an 80% likelihood that users prefer a minimal checkout experience. That does not mean the solution is simply “build a minimal checkout.” Data should function as a compass, not a map.

These questions help designers validate predictions through usability testing and additional research. AI excels at identifying patterns, but it rarely explains why those patterns exist. Understanding motivation is still a human-centered research task.

Recent findings suggest that the clearest cautionary tale here is Amazon’s experimental AI recruitment tool, which the organization reportedly scrapped after discovering that the model had learned to downgrade resumes from women. The training data, roughly a decade of historical hiring decisions, was skewed toward male candidates, and the model inherited that skew. It began penalizing resumes that included the word “women’s,” as in “women’s chess club captain,” and favoring language more commonly found on men’s resumes. The system was not intentionally biased — the data was. Amazon reportedly tried to adjust it and eventually shut the project down because they could not guarantee it would not surface other discriminatory patterns.

It has been revealed that examples like this are why interpreting AI output critically matters. Designers need to understand the data behind a prediction and evaluate the reliability of the models they depend on. A recommendation is only as good as the data it was trained on, and the only way to know what that data is hiding is to ask.

Experimentation is usually framed as a way to validate a design decision. Want to lift the click-through rate of a CTA? Run an A/B test. Probabilistic thinking reframes this. Experiments should not only confirm solutions but also reduce uncertainty.

It has been revealed that traditional A/B testing is expensive. It costs engineering time, traffic allocation, and user exposure, especially when a losing variant runs against a significant chunk of your audience. AI simulations can help filter weaker ideas before they reach production by making experimentation more efficient. User needs shift constantly, and the most effective teams iterate fast.

Recent findings suggest that AI can help evaluate assumptions early by modeling potential outcomes based on historical and behavioral data. These simulations act as a hypothesis filter, pointing to the directions worth investing engineering effort in. This also supports personalization — different users may respond better to different experiences. Version A may resonate with high-intent users while version B works better for exploratory ones. Multiple experiences living side by side are not a flaw; they can be an intentional strategy.

In a recent development, AI amplifies probabilistic thinking by surfacing scenarios, assigning likelihood scores, and enabling personalization at scale. Experimentation becomes a continuous feedback loop:.

Predict → Test → Learn → Adjust → Repeat!

Use this template to define the hypothesis:.

Sources indicate that we believe [behavioral assumption] will impact [metric] because [reason]. We’ll know we are right when [evidence].

Example: We believe simplifying the onboarding flow from 5 steps to 3 will increase completion rate because owners experience decision fatigue when too many choices are presented. We’ll know we’re right when we see at least a 15% increase in step-to-step conversion with no drop in activation rate.

One of the hardest things for designers is making uncertainty understandable and actionable. When uncertainty is hidden, people treat AI outputs as facts. When it’s communicated clearly, trust increases.

Industry observers note that ranges, estimates, and confidence indicators go a long way. A delivery window of “Friday to Monday” tells the truth about variability without misleading anyone, whereas a specific timestamp that slips erodes trust every time. A face recognition feature that notes “this looks like Pratik, is that right?” sets more honest expectations than one that just labels the photo with a name.

It has been revealed that communicating uncertainty does not weaken trust — it strengthens it. The goal is not to eliminate uncertainty but to design for it intelligently.

Different owners respond to uncertainty differently, and your design should account for that:.

Sources indicate that AI should augment human judgment, and certainly not replace it. The most trustworthy systems are designed with clear moments where people can review, challenge, correct, or override machine suggestions. Human-in-the-loop (HITL) is not a safety net — it is a refinement engine. Every override, correction, or rejection becomes high-quality feedback that improves the model over time.

Control is a prerequisite for adoption. Consumers are more willing to rely on AI when they understand how a suggestion was generated, can evaluate its implications, and can easily intervene. Well-designed products make this explicit: who is acting, what happens if the suggestion is wrong, and where the user can step in.

These interactions are also critical for system improvement. Every accept, reject, or edit is a strong signal, and compared to passive analytics, this kind of feedback produces far more meaningful training data. It closes the loop between real-world usage and model performance.

Industry observers note that gitHub Copilot is a good everyday example. It offers inline code suggestions that developers can accept with a tab, edit, or ignore entirely. The system never commits code on the user’s behalf. Authorship stays with the humans. Every data point becomes implicit feedback about which suggestions were useful. Gmail’s Smart Compose works similarly, presenting predicted text as optional, keeping tone and intent in the user’s hands.

Industry observers note that in higher-stakes contexts, HITL becomes more explicit. Risk and fraud systems typically use probability scores to route decisions: low-risk: proceed automatically; medium-risk: trigger additional verification; and high-risk: escalate to a human reviewer. This balances speed with judgment without removing oversight.

In safety-critical domains like healthcare, human oversight is non-negotiable. AI may flag anomalies or suggest a diagnosis, but the clinician retains final authority. Tools that explain the details help the practitioner understand why a recommendation was made, reinforcing confidence without removing accountability.

From a UX perspective, HITL is about matching the interaction pattern to the level of risk. Simple accept/reject affordances work well for low-risk suggestions that improve speed without real consequences. As the stakes climb, impacting data, money, or people, preview and approval steps become essential. Explanations help users calibrate trust rather than blindly accept outputs.

What happens behind the scenes matters just as much. The system should capture user decisions with context, feed them into learning workflows, and log overrides for auditability. Over time, teams can track signals like override rate, confidence accuracy, time-to-approval, and perceived trust. A high override rate is not a user failure. It is a signal that the design or the model needs attention.

In a recent development, poorly implemented HITL systems can fail in subtle ways. Human review can devolve into a rubber stamp. Workflows can slow down so much that users route around the safeguards. Feedback can skew toward a narrow subset of users. These risks are real, but they are design problems, not reasons to remove HITL.

The goal is not to maximize human involvement. It is to focus it where uncertainty, impact, or ethics demand it. Keeping HITL is less about control and more about clarity: clarity about who decides, when uncertainty matters, and how responsibility is shared between people and machines.

Sources indicate that good design adapts as the landscape shifts. Product design, especially in AI-powered systems, can no longer afford to optimize only for short-term conversion metrics. User intent is fluid as well as ever-changing, environments change rapidly, and probabilistic systems continuously evolve too. What works today can quietly break tomorrow. Designing for resilience means building products that stay reliable, trustworthy, and useful even as assumptions, data, and user behaviors change.

Resilient design shifts the question from:.

In a recent development, how do we maximize this metric right now?! → How does this system behave over time, under stress, and in uncertainty?

A resilient system is one that:.

Do not just consider last quarter’s numbers. Peek into the following quarters to identify the shift and make changes accordingly.

Likelihoods shift constantly, AI models drift, contexts evolve, and user needs mature as well, so designing as if conditions are stable creates fragility in probabilistic environments. A resilient approach assumes volatility as the default.

Think about how recommendation systems tend to evolve. The early version of a content feed optimizes for engagement, and for a while, engagement goes up. Then people start to notice the feed feels narrow, repetitive, maybe even exhausting. Resilient systems rebalance, introducing novelty, diversifying signals, and pulling in long-term satisfaction measures alongside short-term clicks.

Short-term conversion gains often hide long-term costs. Speeding up onboarding can reduce comprehension. Maximizing notification CTR can erode trust. Optimizing engagement alone can produce unhealthy usage patterns. Fragile systems maximize numbers while ignoring second-order effects, the downstream consequences that show up weeks or months later.

It has been revealed that duolingo’s hearts system is a good example of designing against this. It introduces friction: if you make too many mistakes, you run out of hearts and have to wait or practice older material to earn more. On paper, that looks like a conversion killer: fewer lessons per session. In practice, the team has publicly discussed how it supports long-term motivation and retention, which is the metric that actually matters for a learning app. Short-term engagement dips, but long-term outcomes improve.

According to recent reports, meta has made a similar, if more reluctant, shift. The tech giant publicly acknowledged that optimizing purely for “time spent” produced unintended emotional and societal effects, which led to a stated pivot toward “meaningful social interactions” as a guiding metric. Whether that shift fully landed is up for debate, but the acknowledgment itself is the point: optimizing for the wrong thing at scale has real downstream cost.

So, designers must routinely ask:.

Recent findings suggest that teams routinely plan for traffic spikes, but rarely for uncertainty spikes. Yet AI systems degrade, adversarial behaviors evolve, and external shocks can reshape user behavior overnight. Resilient design assumes variability and prepares for it.

Recent findings suggest that this means designing for degrading confidence. What does your interface do when the AI isn’t sure? Does it quietly fail, or does it gracefully hand off? Does the experience still make sense if AI assistance goes away entirely? A good fallback strategy is as vital as the happy path.

If you take one thing from this article into your next design review, make it this:.

That single reframe changes how you write hypotheses, interpret AI output, scope experiments, and design for the moments when the system is wrong. Starting this week, name the assumption behind every AI recommendation you accept, find one place in your product where a probabilistic output is presented as a certainty, fix the framing, and design the fallback before the happy path.

In a recent development, the shift from deterministic to probabilistic design is less about new tools and more about a new posture. AI has not introduced uncertainty into our world. It has simply made the uncertainty that was always there impossible to ignore. AI can estimate, simulate, and recommend, but it cannot decide what matters, which customers are being overlooked, or which unconventional idea is worth defending against a model trained on yesterday’s data. Those remain human responsibilities. Think in ranges, not points. Test assumptions, not features. Build for adaptation, not perfection. In a world where prediction is cheap, and judgment is rare, the most valuable thing a designer can do is keep asking, What else might be true?

Ray Gun Magazine: The Design That Broke Every Rule

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (416 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Abduzeedo

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ray Gun magazine rolled out in November 1992 and tore up the rulebook of editorial design, with David Carson turning type into image.
  • Sources indicate that the premiere problem sets the tone on the cover alone.
  • Carson was a former professional surfer with no formal design training, and he designed like it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ray Gun magazine rolled out in November 1992 and tore up the rulebook of editorial design, with David Carson turning type into image.

Sources indicate that the premiere problem sets the tone on the cover alone. The masthead reads rAY GUn in oversized red letters, off-kilter and cropped by the page edge. A photocopied portrait of Henry Rollins is torn across the cover, and the contents run down the left side in a typewriter face. Publisher Marvin Scott Jarrett started the magazine with three people in the dining room of his one-bedroom apartment, and the design matches that beginning. It looks assembled by hand, not laid out on a grid. Blue duotone, scratched film, hand-scrawled headlines. The magazine looks the way the music sounds.

Carson was a former professional surfer with no formal design training, and he designed like it. His most famous move came in 1994, when he set an entire Bryan Ferry interview in Zapf Dingbats because he found the interview boring. The symbols fill the spread, with a green portrait of Ferry slumped in a chair and one giant red dingbat floating above it. His line on the work was simple: don't mistake legibility for communication. The same instinct runs through the first issue. The word RAVE is split across a spread in letters that fill the page. The headline for the rock star piece scatters its letters down the page. One article is piled into a solid block of black type. The page is a single expressive surface, and the reader has to work to read it. That friction was the design.

The texture comes from the making: photocopied collage, contact sheets, torn edges, duotone photography, type cut and pasted by hand. It reads as a zine printed at magazine scale, and that roughness carried the magazine past Carson too. He left after issue 30, the October 1995 David Bowie cover. Robert Hales took over, then Chris Ashworth took the design from 1997, later sharing the role with Amanda Sissons, with a harder, distressed look they called Swiss Grit.

The masthead kept changing color and weight, green on issue 12, white on black on the Perry Farrell cover. Ray Gun ran over 70 problems and closed in January 2000. Its influence outlived it. A generation of designers learned the grid was a choice, not a law, and Carson's book The End of Print carried the argument into design schools everywhere.

See more of David Carson's work at davidcarsondesign.com.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that this past summer, the Newark Museum of Art in Fresh Jersey initiated a dialogue with the family of David Drake (around 1801-74), the enslaved potter from South Carolina, regarding a large brown ceramic jug in its collection, dated 1852. Just a few months later—lightning speed in museum time—The Art Newspaper has learned that the institution has reached an agreement with Drake’s heirs to restore ownership of the work and purchase it back for its permanent collection.

The arrangement comes just over a year after the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston reached an historic agreement with Drake’s family to return two major stoneware vessels, one of which the museum purchased back. Momentum built from there and return agreements were reached with institutions including the Telfair Museums in Savannah and the Georgia Museum of Art in Athens, Georgia, the Virginia Museum of Fine Arts, and others.

It has been revealed that “What happened this July was really special,” says George Fatheree, an adviser to the Drake family. A letter the Newark Museum sent to the artist’s descendants and shared with The Art Newspaper states: “We acquired a jug by your ancestor in 2022 to help us more powerfully teach the history of enslavement and enslaved labour, as part of the 2023 reimagining and reinstallation of our American art galleries, Seeing America: 18th and 19th Century.” Noting the MFA Boston partnership, the museum extended the opportunity to meet and “identify ways we might collaborate”.

According to Lisa Funderburke, the Newark Museum’s director and chief executive, it was the museum’s senior director of registration and collections management, Amber Germano, who first approached her over the summer and asked if she would be willing to sign a letter.

“It’s not uncommon for curators to visit my office with a stack of papers of things that are either for consideration or ongoing engagement on articles of repatriation,” Funderburke says. “Always my first question is: ‘Can you articulate to me what we’re doing here and what the impulse behind that is?’”.

In a recent development, according to Yaba Baker, one of Drake’s fourth great-grandsons, Funderburke credited her staff with the initial action. “Lisa understood immediately what needed to be done,” Baker notes. “One thing my family all agreed on: Dave is such a powerful figure in art history and Black history that to take the pots out of public view would be a disservice.”.

Recent findings suggest that things moved rapidly after that, with additional family meetings and Funderburke’s conversations with board members and other leaders at the museum. “I felt like this would be a strong north star for our board about where we are and where we want to be, and position ourselves as a museum into the future,” the director says.

After the museum commissioned several appraisals of the ceramic vessel, a value of around $135,000 was decided on. Numerous Drake pots have sold for five- and six-figure prices; the current record at auction for one of his works is the $1.65m paid for his 25-Gallon Poem Jar (1858), achieved at Crocker Farm Auctions in Maryland in 2021.

“Our approach is this should not be a zero-sum game,” Fatheree says, describing the outcome in Newark as a “win-win”.

Baker concurs, stressing the enduring lessons of Drake’s legacy. “He was a slave. He was considered three fifths of a person by the US constitution,” Baker notes, adding that anti-literacy laws in South Carolina at the time forbade teaching enslaved people to write.

“For our family, it’s telling the story of someone who was considered by a lot of people to be nothing, but he conducted himself with such excellence,” Baker states, before quoting a famous inscription Drake wrote on another of his vessels that begins, “I wonder where is all my relation”, and concludes: “Friendship to all.”.

Latest Update: Why Accessibility Is An Operational Capability, Not A Feature

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
