Shanghai’s art week finds buyers in a selective market

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1017 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Shanghai’s two leading art fairs, West Bund Art & Design and Art021, opened this week against a backdrop of slowing economic growth, subdued confidence in China’s art market and an increasingly crowded international art calendar.
  • It has been revealed that “I think the serious people who have a long-term idea of what they want to do, they keep collecting,” says René Meile, director of Galerie Urs Meile, which has a location in Beijing.
  • Meanwhile this year’s art week brings an explosion of art events city-wide and boasts many newcomers both in terms of industry visitors and latest spaces, including three new galleries.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Shanghai’s two leading art fairs, West Bund Art & Design and Art021, opened this week against a backdrop of slowing economic growth, subdued confidence in China’s art market and an increasingly crowded international art calendar. While the city no longer commands the same international panache it enjoyed before the pandemic, galleries report encouraging early sales, suggesting that committed collectors remain active despite a more cautious market.

It has been revealed that “I think the serious people who have a long-term idea of what they want to do, they keep collecting,” says René Meile, director of Galerie Urs Meile, which has a location in Beijing. He adds that younger collectors increasingly favour artists of their own generation. While established artists continued to attract buyers, collectors were taking longer to commit to expensive works. Meile attributed the shift partly to the departure of speculative buyers from the market.

Meanwhile this year’s art week brings an explosion of art events city-wide and boasts many newcomers both in terms of industry visitors and latest spaces, including three new galleries. Hangzhou’s longtime fair regular Inna Art Space just opened Inna Front Room in the Lujiazui business district, making it the first significant gallery on the Pudong side of the river. Chen Yongwei, the former director of nonprofit Pond Society, has opened Shanghai Industry atop the Suhe House art cluster. PTT Space, a rising star gallery from Taipei, meanwhile this week opened an outpost at the M50 gallery complex.

Recent findings suggest that “Even though the Chinese market is at an all-time low, Shanghai is still a vibrant international city with many art institutions,” indicates Robert Hsu, who founded PTT in 2020. “Considering the past art week, the number of openings parties and fairs is still through the roof, surpassing Seoul Art Week and coming close to Hong Kong Art Week.”.

Hsu indicates he also has existing “base infrastructure” in the city with staff and relationships with local artists and collectors. “As a second generation gallerist, I feel we have to keep moving in this newly introduced era. The market, the business, the people have all changed. To survive, I have to step out of our comfort zone and explore.”.

Jae Pil Eun's Night Walking, showing at Hang Over.

Courtesy of the artists and SYSTEMA © SYSTEMA, 2026.

In a recent development, along with the gallery, Hsu is part of the team organising the new boutique fair Art Fusion Canton in the southern Chinese city Guangzhou next month (3-7 December). In Shanghai, the popup fair Hang Over (11-15 November) is going strong in its second year. Moving from last year’s restaurant to an event space in a new lifestyle complex on Donghu Lu, it this year features 18 galleries including Tokyo’s Misako & Rosen, Seoul’s Cylinder along with Shanghai’s Antenna Space, Vanguard and Linseed, owned by Hang Over founder Zhuang Lingzhi.

The 13th edition of West Bund Art & Design (10–15 November) brought together 85 galleries, including Hauser & Wirth, Perrotin, Thaddaeus Ropac and White Cube. Meanwhile, the 14th Art021, hosting 111 galleries at the Shanghai Exhibition Centre, has introduced a new acquisition initiative with the Los Angeles County Museum of Art (Lacma), supported by Chinese collectors, aimed at bringing works by Asian and Asian diaspora artists into the museum’s collection.

At West Bund, Thaddaeus Ropac reports several opening-day sales, led by Megan Rooney’s That Sky (Atlas) (2026), sold for £400,000 to a Chinese foundation. Other transactions included a painting by Martha Jungwirth for €200,000, a Robert Longo work for $90,000 and a painting by Han Bing for €55,000, acquired by an Asian museum. A work by Joan Snyder was also sold to a Chinese museum.

Visitor at West Bund Art & Design 2026.

Courtesy of West Bund Art & Design.

Dawn Zhu, the gallery’s Asia director, praises the enthusiasm of collectors, noting that the gallery had made early sales to both institutions and private collections. “We are seeing collectors who have travelled from across South East Asia and even a few from Europe,” she states.

Hauser & Wirth also reports significant sales at West Bund, led by Louise Bourgeois’s bronze sculpture Point of Contact (1967–68, cast 2006), which sold for $450,000 to a museum in Kuala Lumpur. Other transactions include Lee Bul’s Perdu XXXIII (2020), sold for $260,000 to a private collection in China, and another Bourgeois work, Femme (2008), acquired by a Chinese private collector for $165,000. The gallery also reports the sale of George Condo’s Black and Red Composition (2026) for $200,000.

At Art021, Galerie Urs Meile reports sales of works by Xie Nanxing for approximately RMB 1.2m and Ju Ting for RMB 400,000, alongside works by younger artists Chen Zuo and Miao Miao priced between RMB 100,000 and RMB 150,000, and a smaller painting by Vietnamese artist Mai Ta for RMB 40,000.

Also at Art021, Shanghai-based gallery Bank reports strong early sales of Liang Hao’s works, priced 60,000 to 300,000 RMB, and of a large Jiang Cheng painting for over 500,000 RMB. The gallery reports that Lacma may acquire a video work made in 2000 by Los Angeles-based artist Patty Chang.

Despite the more subdued atmosphere, some galleries remain optimistic about the depth of China’s domestic market. Liang Xiao, a spokesperson for Perrotin, which has operated a Shanghai space since 2018, says that the slowdown had given collectors more time to select works they genuinely appreciate.

Recent findings suggest that he suggests that the growth of newly introduced art fairs in Yokohama, Seoul and elsewhere would not fundamentally undermine Shanghai’s position, given the size of China’s domestic collector base. “Even after all these years, there are still many collectors we have yet to reach,” Liang notes, adding that Shanghai remains an important entry point for collectors from across mainland China.

Industry observers note that hsu says the feedback for PTT Shanghai has been “quite positive” in the debut week, but “the market is not at its best.” Transactions have been slow, but included some successful placement of works with established collectors. “As the old saying goes, the gallery business is a marathon, not a sprint.”.

Business Class Product Worldwide.

In a recent development, picture this: you're seated in a private suite at 38,000 feet somewhere over the Atlantic, your door clicked shut behind you, a glass of Dom Pérignon on the side table, and a fully flat bed dressed in Westin Heavenly bedding waiting for you. Your partner is in the suite next to yours — and when you lower the center dividing panel, you're sharing a meal in what Qatar Airways calls the "Double Bed" configuration. This is QSuites, and it is, without exaggeration, the single most celebrated business class product in the world. Now here's the number that stops the ChooseFI community cold: a cash ticket in QSuites from New York JFK to Doha DOH typically runs **$5,000 to $10,000 per person**. That's a mortgage payment. That's a family vacation budget. That's real money that compounds in an index fund. With Qatar Avios through the Privilege Club program, that same seat costs **75,000 Avios**. When you do the math against even the conservative cash price of $5,000, you're extracting **6.7 cents per point**. Against the top-end cash price of $10,000, that's **13.3 cents per point** — in a world where most loyalty currencies are "worth" 1 cent each. This is a 6x to 13x multiplier on every point you've earned. Here's what makes this a genuine pricing inefficiency rather than just marketing: Qatar's award chart is fixed and partner-friendly, meaning the number of points required doesn't scale dynamically with cash prices the way most airline programs now do. When demand spikes and cash fares hit $10,000, your award price stays exactly 75,000 Avios. The loyalty program hasn't caught up to the revenue management engine, and that gap is your opportunity. For anyone on the path to financial independence, this is the travel rewards philosophy in its purest form: redirect real spending you're already doing onto the right cards, accumulate points as a byproduct, and convert those points into experiences that would otherwise require liquidating investments. The QSuites redemption is the pinnacle of that system — a **nearly free** business class experience that delivers more luxury per point than almost anything else in the world of travel rewards.

The mechanism behind this sweet spot is elegant once you see it, and once you see it, you'll start recognizing similar patterns everywhere in the loyalty space.

Qatar prices its own flights in its own currency — and that currency is cheap to acquire.

Qatar Airways Privilege Club Avios are the program's native points currency. When Qatar sets award prices for its own operated flights, including QSuites, it prices them in a way that's competitive and fixed — not subject to the dynamic pricing algorithms that have made programs like United MileagePlus or Delta SkyMiles increasingly unpredictable. Seventy-five thousand Avios for a transatlantic or transoceanic business class seat is a published, stable price. Qatar isn't trying to extract maximum value from every award booking; they want to keep the program attractive to drive loyalty.

The critical insight is this: you don't need to earn Qatar Avios through Qatar flights. You can transfer them directly from credit card programs you're probably already using.

According to recent reports, citi ThankYou Points → Qatar Avios at 1:1 — This is the fastest and cleanest route. Transfers from Citi to Qatar are instant, meaning you can search for availability, confirm the seat is bookable, and transfer in the same session without risk. For anyone holding a Citi Premier or Citi Prestige card, this is a direct pipeline to QSuites.

Capital One Miles → Qatar Avios at 1:1 — A strong secondary option. Venture X and Venture card holders have access to this path.

In a recent development, marriott Bonvoy Points → Qatar Avios at 3:1 — This is the least efficient path. In a recent development, this is a huge deal that deserves its own callout. Qatar charges zero fuel surcharges on Qatar-operated award flights. With Qatar Privilege Club, what you see is what you pay: 75,000 Avios plus the government taxes, which are typically modest.

The stopover rule turns a single award redemption into a multi-destination experience, a classic FI travel rewards optimization move.

According to recent reports, this is the cardinal rule of all transfer-based award bookings: never transfer points until you've confirmed the seat exists. Go to qatarairways.com and run a search using the "Privilege Club" award booking tool. Select Business Class, enter your route (e.g., JFK to DOH), and look for QSuites availability specifically — you'll see the aircraft type and cabin configuration in the search results. QSuites is typically available on Boeing 777-300ER and A380 flights, not all Qatar aircraft, so confirm the product before you get excited.

Qatar Privilege Club opens its award booking window at 361 days in advance. QSuites availability is genuinely limited — this is a Difficulty 2/5 on the availability scale — and the best seats disappear quickly, especially for peak travel periods and popular routes like JFK–DOH. Set a calendar reminder now for exactly 361 days before your target departure date and be ready to book the moment the window opens. This single habit separates people who get QSuites awards from people who watch them disappear.

In a recent development, if you can't find two seats together, try splitting the booking into two single-seat reservations, then request to link them. Calling Qatar's Privilege Club phone line (rather than booking online) occasionally surfaces inventory not shown on the website.

In a recent development, british Airways Avios uses a distance-based award chart rather than a flat-rate chart, which creates a pricing inefficiency on long-haul routes operated by Qatar Airways. While BA prices short-haul flights competitively, flights over 4,000 miles to Qatar and beyond land in a pricing band that dramatically undervalues the QSuites product. Qatar Airways is a oneworld alliance member, which means BA Avios can book any Qatar-operated award flight. The key insight is that you are booking through BA's system using BA's pricing, but flying on Qatar's hardware — and Qatar's business class product is in a completely different league than BA's Club World. This mismatch between the booking partner's award chart and the operating airline's product quality is exactly what makes this a sweet spot.

  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • So what icon is the most reliable to show expansion and collapsing for accordions?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that vitaly Friedman loves beautiful content and doesn’t like to give in easily. When he is not writing, he’s most probably running front-end & UX … More about Vitaly ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

So what icon is the most reliable to show expansion and collapsing for accordions? Is there really any noticeable difference between carets, chevrons, arrows, and triangles?

Industry observers note that well, research demonstrates that there is some difference indeed. But what’s more interesting is that split menus are harmful, why it’s better to not have icons and text labels link to different actions, and why the caret is the safest icon choice. Let’s dive in!

The findings aren’t very surprising: without any icon in use, customers expect that tapping on the menu item would take them directly to a upcoming page. Users often struggle with custom icons as they don’t clearly signal that they’ll open an accordion. And people tend to tap fairly equally on the icon and on the label for most icons.

Industry observers note that many designs (like the one below) tend to slightly overcomplicate things by adding arrows and carets pointing everywhere, depending on the state of the accordion. But typically we don’t need to use an arrow to indicate a link to the category.

The rule of thumb is very simple: if it’s a link, the easiest and most effective way is to simply underline it — without any arrow, caret, or other icon. Perhaps it’s not particularly exciting, but it works flawlessly every single time.

Using a right-facing arrow icon ▶ isn’t associated with an expectation of going directly to a latest page. And having the same icon pointing down ▼ doesn’t necessarily imply that an accordion is going to open on tap/click.

In a recent development, it’s a good idea to avoid split buttons for accordions — where the text label links directly to a page, but the icon opens the accordion. Instead, it’s much more reliable to allow people to tap on a main category and expose the menu; and to access the category page, we add a link to it inside the menu.

In a recent development, for accordions, we typically use +/− or arrows ↓/↑ to signal expanded and collapsed states, and typically it works well. However, both have many different interpretations. Plus + can mean anything from saving for later to adding to cart to zooming in, and can be particularly confusing for multi-level navigation, with many levels open at the same time.

According to recent reports, arrows ↓/↑ can mean scrolling or sliding or finding the next match, but also a jump to a particular portion of a page. Both plus and arrows are well-understood and work, but depending on the design, can be confusing — mostly because they are overloaded.

The safe choice is to use the caret/triangle pointing down ▼ by default, and change it to a caret pointing up or a caret pointing sideways ▶ on interaction. If you need an alternative, then +/- typically work well, too.

Sources indicate that but we certainly don’t need any further icons or arrows to indicate where the links go. The same goes for split menus, which often produce more mistakes than help. Instead, we have one button or dropdown that does exactly one thing — highlights all options and allows users to drill down.

And if you need a direct link, we link the title directly to the page and underline it. More often than not, simpler is better.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Barkas builds the Kuda brand identity on More Life: a stacked wordmark, custom Kuda Modena type, and a deep Lagos purple.

The system starts from a sentence, not a logo. "If your bank isn't helping you live more, it's holding you back," Barkas writes, and the identity answers with the pulse of Lagos: a stacked KUDA wordmark in thick geometric capitals, deep purple owning every surface it touches, black as its sharper counterweight. Kuda began as "the bank of the free," challenging the friction and fees of traditional Nigerian banking, and the newly introduced work keeps that challenger spirit, aimed at a generation that wants its money to fund a life rather than sit in an account.

Recent findings suggest that the type does the heavy lifting. Kuda Modena, a custom face drawn by Erkin Karamemet, sets the name at poster scale in heavy geometric capitals for the wordmark and the More Life lockups, with Suisse International alongside for support. The specimen highlights the full alphabet in lilac on deep purple, with the custom Naira sign sitting among the euro, dollar, pound, and yen, a small detail that roots the whole system in Nigerian money.

According to recent reports, the grid is the app itself. The home screen sorts everything into three plain groups, Essentials, Cardless Payments, and Lifestyle, each icon labeled in the same weight. The wordmark stacks KU over DA like a stamp, and the studio built four versions of the lockup so the mark stays legible from a billboard down to a card chip. Posters hold the same discipline: one line, one color field, the name at the foot.

It has been revealed that purple is the material here. Deep purple fields carry the type, the app, and the card, with lilac doing the bright work and black stepping in wherever the brand needs to sound serious, which is how Kuda Business reads against the personal product. Hand-drawn illustrations soften the geometry: a Lagos street scene in colored pencil, a woman in a pink robe on the SPEND card, loose doodles of everyday moments. Documentary photography from local photographers keeps the people real and unfiltered.

Sources indicate that the system stretches across every surface the bank touches. Three phone screens show the balance, the lilac card, and a PIN pad in one calm row. A billboard puts the stacked wordmark over a woman waving from a car window with the line "Less friction. More life." The stocks screen tracks a holding in dollars on the same purple field. Nothing in the system looks like a bank trying to look expensive; everything looks like a bank trying to keep up with Lagos.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the University of California, San Diego will open a 12,000-sq.-ft contemporary art space on its campus in spring 2027.
  • Jessica Berlanga Taylor, UC San Diego’s chief campus curator, tells The Art Newspaper that the university is aware of the challenges other San Diego cultural institutions are facing and believes investing in art and culture is essential.
  • It has been revealed that in 2023, the local philanthropists Matthew and Iris Strauss gave more than 100 works form their art collection to UC San Diego.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the University of California, San Diego will open a 12,000-sq.-ft contemporary art space on its campus in spring 2027. Housed in the university’s new Triton Center, the Strauss Family Gallery will include four indoor exhibition spaces and an outdoor sculpture terrace. Free and open to the public, the Strauss will host exhibitions, commissions, artist residencies and public programmes that encourage collaboration between artists and UC San Diego researchers and scholars.

Jessica Berlanga Taylor, UC San Diego’s chief campus curator, tells The Art Newspaper that the university is aware of the challenges other San Diego cultural institutions are facing and believes investing in art and culture is essential. "The Strauss represents a long-term commitment that the university is making to contemporary art and sees it as an integral part of the university's intellectual and public life," she notes.

It has been revealed that in 2023, the local philanthropists Matthew and Iris Strauss gave more than 100 works form their art collection to UC San Diego. (Matthew, who made his money in real estate, died the following year.) Represented artists in the gift include Carrie Mae Weems, Fred Wilson, Zhang Huan and Sabine Moritz.

The Strauss’s latest David and Claire Guggenheim Gallery will serve as the public entrance and a space for exhibitions, gatherings and an artist-in-residence programme focused on digital artists, while the two-story Gray Box will accommodate large-scale sculpture, moving-image installations and performances.

The 3,043-sq.-ft Black Box will be equipped for immersive video, sound, sculpture and performance; and the White Cube will provide a more conventional gallery setting for works from the Strauss Family Foundation, travelling exhibitions and collaborations with collections in San Diego and beyond.

Taylor calls the Strauss the first "ground-up museum" at UC San Diego. Pointing to existing spaces on campus like the Mandeville Art Gallery (open for nearly 60 years) and a black-box theatre in the music department, she says the Strauss will strive to be part of the landscape of both the campus and San Diego at large. But the Strauss will play a unique role—with commissions, curatorial research and exhibitions in collaboration with artists from across the globe.

In a recent development, UC San Diego’s Stuart Collection, which includes sculptures installed across campus, has already established a public art presence at the university. The Strauss will now give artists a dedicated space for exhibitions, commissions and research.

In a recent development, “We’re connecting art inside with art outside now with the Strauss and the Stuart Collection, but we also want to distinguish very clearly what Stuart is about and what the Strauss will achieve," Taylor says. "The Strauss is very much about perception and experience, but it’s also about expanding our ways of knowing and presenting different forms of knowledge that you wouldn’t necessarily encounter in the classroom.".

Taylor's greater vision is to engage the community through public programming and student involvement. The Strauss looks to engage both established and emerging artists, particularly in the digital space, and support the development of their work. "We're looking at how we can bring artistic inquiry into university teaching and research," Taylor states.

It has been revealed that this could include incorporating exhibitions and artistic methodologies into existing courses, giving students opportunities to participate in curatorial research and creative projects, and developing collaborations across the university. Taylor points to potential partnerships with UC San Diego’s Qualcomm Institute, the Interdisciplinary Computing and the Arts programme, the Scripps Institution of Oceanography and the Goeddel Family Technology Sandbox as examples of the range of possibilities.

"We see the Strauss as more of a platform than a container for a collection," Taylor notes. "We do have a collection, but our goal is to be a platform for research and critical inquiry—and for challenging assumptions.".

Twenty years changes a grudge. Early in his career in Aotearoa, Kris Sowersby wrestled with bÃ©zier curves in FontLab and bought into Typophile forum dogma claiming Helvetica didnât work for serious reading. Still, he kept circling its gravity across Calibre, Untitled Sans, SÃ¶hne, and Founders Grotesk, sneaking Helveticaâs weight and spacing into a family that remained a bestseller twelve years later. Facing that 70-year shadow head-on meant accepting what graphic designers like Massimo Vignelli and Experimental Jetset already knew: a workhorse font isnât finished until people put it to work.

Negative tracking always cheats the curves. Itâs Klimâs first public variable font, built after moving engineering to GitHub, fontmake, and Designspace, and it pairs a disciplined neo-grotesque type skeleton with a dedicated Optical Size axis. Dragging the opsz slider from 6pt up to 42pt tightens or loosens letterfit for the intended point size automatically. Right below the opening collage, white Die Grotesk design information headlines lock against a stark black header with that exact tight-but-not-touching tension. Sowersby tuned those Die Grotesk D cuts specifically for one- or two-word logotypes and posters â sparing designers the crude habit of crushing sidebearings by hand.

Industry observers note that small text demands a different temperament. Studying physical 8, 9, and 10pt Haas metal specimens demonstrated Sowersby how calm and even Helveticaâs early grey texture looked before first-generation digital conversions flattened it, shaping the sympathetic spacing of Die Grotesk A. Across the 3,625-word essay, hand-drawn red asterisks and narrow margin footnotes break up candid reflections on corporate font monopolies, takeaway menu boards in Waikanae, and functional neutrality. That everyday utility carries straight into the burnt-orange specimen frames, where bold black Die Grotesk lettering and a moulded plastic monobloc chair sit above a single interactive slider. Good neo-grotesque type doesnât beg for attention. It holds up on a laminated rate card or a gallery wall with equal composure.

Modern CSS Might Make Your Front-End More Complex

📅 2026-11-03 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3325 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • Have you ever replaced fifty lines of JavaScript with a few lines of CSS, merged the PR, and felt like you just did the codebase a favor?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gabriel is a front-end developer and technical writer. He specializes in HTML, CSS, JavaScript, React, Vue, TailwindCSS, and BootStrap, with a track record of … More about Gabriel ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

Have you ever replaced fifty lines of JavaScript with a few lines of CSS, merged the PR, and felt like you just did the codebase a favor? You replace ResizeObserver with a container query, the diff is mostly red, and everyone approves it before lunch.

This was what it looked like before you made the change:.

See the Pen [demo (before PR) [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/XJMxVJq) by Shoyombo Gabriel Ayomide.

It has been revealed that then, a week later, a card on the dashboard has vanished. A heading has grown on tablets for no reason anyone can explain. The spacing inside a comment is off.

See the Pen [demo (after PR) [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/gbmBopp) by Shoyombo Gabriel Ayomide.

Recent findings suggest that none of these bugs are in the few lines you wrote. All of them arrived with those few lines of CSS.

It has been revealed that in my last article on how CSS is growing smarter, I left a few questions hanging at the end, including: What happens when logic is split between CSS and JavaScript, and how do we debug conditional styles without a clear view of what triggered them? This article is my attempt to answer these two questions.

I think it’s worth saying clearly that I am not saying modern CSS is bad. What I am saying is that:.

A CSS feature can simplify a piece of code while making the wider application harder to reason about if you don’t understand how it relates to existing code, be it CSS or JavaScript.

Think of a new CSS feature as a new tenant moving into a shared apartment. The tenant may be quiet and tidy, but they still share a kitchen with everyone who already lives there. In that case, CSS is now roommates with JavaScript, the component’s layout, the CSS Cascade, and the browser’s rendering engine. The apartment’s stability depends less on the tenant and more on how they get along with one another.

That gives us two different things to measure, and a diff only indicates the first one:.

According to recent reports, I am not the only one thinking about this. In April 2026, Igor Roztropiński published an essay titled “Modern Frontend Complexity: essential or accidental?” asking:.

Recent findings suggest that the essay landed on r/programming, where the thread has drawn 80-plus comments and the replies pull in two directions. One of the most upvoted comments, from a user named Kwantuum, pushes back on the whole genre:.

Another commenter, kayinfire, takes the other side, arguing that “there are tons of scenarios where a front-end framework introduces more accidental complexity than it’s worth.” They say this a few replies later:.

I think both commenters are on to something, and this article lives in the gap between the two. Yes, CSS has improved in the last several years. And yes, “less” CSS on paper is not automatically “less” complexity in practice. That said, my claim is narrower. A native feature only reduces complexity when it actually replaces what was there before and doesn’t disrupt the calm state of everything else it interacts with.

Let’s meet the housemates in our metaphorical apartment, one scenario at a time.

The first housemate is JavaScript, and the trouble starts when the old tenant never quite moves out. Here is a card that switches to a two-column layout when it has enough room. The original version uses a ResizeObserver to toggle a class:.

With CSS Container Queries, we need no script at all and can simplify our selectors at the same time:.

According to recent reports, lovely. Now, here’s the thing: migrations rarely happen in one clean sweep. The pull request adds the @container rule and removes the .card--wide .card__body rule. The observer survives because it is registered in another file. The .card--wide .card__title rule survives because nobody searched for the class. Nothing looks broken, because both implementations agree on 480px. Then a designer asks to move the breakpoint to 600px, and a developer updates the only place they know about: the @container rule.

See the Pen [Scenario 1: The Behaviour With Two Owners [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/ZYeqvpx) by Shoyombo Gabriel Ayomide.

Between 480px and 600px, the card now has a single-column body and a wide-layout title. Nobody wrote that state. To find it, you need to know that the layout has two owners and read both of them.

The same trap comes in other shapes:.

CSS and JavaScript can happily share a component. What they cannot share is the component’s behavior. So, instead of having a silent fight over a component’s behavior, check first. Know all the contending parties, then split the work.

Recent findings suggest that and when you’re done migrating, you have to finish the job: delete the observer, the class, and every selector that mentions the class. Otherwise, you may wind up with a tenant who simply refuses to move out.

It has been revealed that back in 2023, I wrote about how block formatting contexts solve float concerns. Back then, creating a block formatting context was something we did on purpose. Today, you can create one without meaning to. When we declare container-type: inline-size, we think we are saying, “let my children query my width.” The browser hears quite a bit more. This is the second housemate, the layout around the component, and our new tenant who just asked for one shelf has ended up rearranging the living room.

According to MDN’s container-type reference, the value “applies style and inline-size containment to the element.” And MDN’s guide to block formatting contexts lists “query containers (elements where container-type isn’t normal)” among the CSS styles that create one. An element that establishes a new block formatting context will, in MDN’s words:.

Sources indicate that that means one declaration can change three layout behaviors that have nothing to do with queries, plus a fourth that comes from inline-size containment. I built a demo where each “before” and “after” pair differs by only that one declaration.

See the Pen [Scenario 2: The Card That Vanished [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/dPvgJpB) by Shoyombo Gabriel Ayomide.

A paragraph with margin-bottom: 16px sits above the card, and the card’s heading has margin-top: 24px. Before the change, the heading’s margin collapsed through the top of the card and merged with the paragraph’s margin, leaving a 24px gap. Afterward, the margin remained trapped inside the card. The two margins now add up to 40px, and the card grows from 30px to 54px tall.

The card follows a floated image. Before the change, the card’s box ran behind the float and its text wrapped around the image. Afterward, the whole card sits beside the float; it starts 120px further in (the width of the image) and is 120px narrower.

This is the one that makes cards vanish. Inline-size containment stops an element from taking its width from its contents. MDN has a nice, succinct explanation:.

Sources indicate that in the last demo, three tag-sized cards sit in a flex row and measure roughly 74px, 96px, and 114px, respectively. If we add container-type: inline-size, then all three measure 0px. I got the same 0px result when the card was displayed inline-block, floated, set to a width: fit-content box, was an align-items: flex-start child of a column flex container, and when it was an item in an auto grid track. A plain block-level card retains its full width because its width is determined by its parent rather than its contents.

Industry observers note that in isolation, the card is a block that fills its parent. In reality, it is a flex item, follows a float, or sits under a paragraph whose margin it used to absorb.

Before you add container-type to an element, ask yourself the following three questions:.

Answering these will help prevent a housemate from completely changing the furniture layout right from under you.

The third housemate is the CSS Cascade. Every shared apartment has house rules about who gets the last word, and a new tenant can arrive with more say than anyone expected.

The :has() selector and native nesting let us write short selectors in CSS. But short selectors can match more and weigh more than they appear.

It has been revealed that say we want to remove paragraph margins from card components that have a hero image. This might look like it does the job:.

See the Pen [Scenario 3: The Selector That Reached Too Far [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/pvexpRd) by Shoyombo Gabriel Ayomide.

According to recent reports, this card has no hero image. Yet every paragraph in it loses its margin.

If you inspect the comment’s paragraph in DevTools and look at the “Styles” pane, you will find two culprits:.

According to recent reports, it could get even more complex and difficult to catch because the state changes at runtime. Let’s say a user posts a comment that includes an avatar. The body text of the card above it loses its spacing. Good luck reproducing that from a bug report that says “spacing looks off sometimes.”.

The fix is to constrain the selector with child combinators:.

This helps the selector get more specific about what it is yelling about.

In a recent development, native nesting has the same habit. MDN’s guide to nesting and specificity says the & selector takes “the largest specificity in the associated selector list,” exactly like :is(). Look at this adaptation of MDN’s example:.

A .button link inside a .card is blue, even though the #featured ID is nowhere near it. The usual reaction is a more specific .button rule, then an exception to that rule. Before you know it, you are in a war of specificity you never knew you had declared.

The way out is to keep the selector list and drop its weight by wrapping it in :where():.

According to recent reports, plain links inside a card are still blue, and the .button link is red again. Again, another way to quiet the loud housemate.

Industry observers note that don’t be fooled into thinking specificity is the whole story. MDN’s introduction to the cascade puts origin, importance, and cascade layers ahead of specificity, and notes that “normal layered styles have less precedence than normal unlayered styles.” In my test, a layered rule with a specificity of 0-4-0 lost to an unlayered .title (0-1-0). So if your new component styles go into @layer components while the legacy stylesheet stays unlayered, the legacy rule wins every conflict, however carefully you wrote the new one. The exception is when the !notable keyword is used, because it actually reverses the cascade order.

According to recent reports, miriam Suzanne’s original proposal for cascade layers describes exactly the pain layers were meant to remove: having to “be very careful with matching specificity to layer.” Layers do remove it, but only when the rules on both sides of the conflict are layered. A half-layered codebase just gives you one more ordering to keep in your head.

Recent findings suggest that none of these battles started with :has() or nesting. In an r/webdev thread titled “CSS-in-JS: What’s the biggest performance drop you actually felt?”, one of the most upvoted answers isn’t about performance at all. It is about the cascade:.

This is about the “order of appearance,” which is the last step in the cascade that ends up deciding a conflict nobody knew existed. Another commenter in the subreddit adds that the injected styles can land in a different order in development and production builds: “Who doesn’t love debugging something that works locally but not in prod.”.

Not everyone in the thread agrees on who is to blame. TheThirdRace replies, “It’s a coding issue, not a technology issue.”.

Industry observers note that I think both are right, and that is exactly the point. CSS-in-JS is a different technology from the native features we are looking at, so take this as a neighboring example, not as proof. But the shape of the problem is the same: the tool did what it promised, and the trouble arose from how it complied with the existing rules.

Sources indicate that “We moved it to CSS, so it’s faster now.” You have probably heard this in a code review, and maybe said it yourself. In my last article, I warned that it isn’t always the case. Let’s test it.

Moving a behavior from JavaScript to CSS changes who does the work. It doesn’t tell you how much work there is. The last housemate, the browser’s rendering engine, is the one who gets the bill. Everyone in the apartment shares it, and nobody looks at it after the move.

Take :has() as an example. Browser vendors were worried about its cost from the start. In a CSS Working Group problem about :has() restrictions, Emilio Cobos Álvarez noted that implementations wanted to ship it with limitations “in order to prevent performance footguns and complexity.” Today, MDN’s :has() page has a whole section on performance with two pieces of advice:.

I wanted numbers, so I built a list with 5,000 rows. The test toggles an .is-selected class on the same row 300 times, so the row’s selected state changes on every toggle, and forces a style and layout update each time. I ran it in Chrome 153 on a Mac in October 2026, and recorded a trace in DevTools to count how many elements each toggle restyles.

See the Pen [Scenario 4: The Rewrite Nobody Measured [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/XJMxVgP) by Shoyombo Gabriel Ayomide.

There are two lessons in that table.

Sources indicate that first, the “bad” selector was fine. Rule 2 is exactly the shape MDN warns against: a :has() anchored to body. It cost about a millisecond and a half more than the script, and it restyled a single element, the toolbar. A frame at 60Hz lasts 16.7ms, so I would take that trade for deleting an event handler any day.

According to recent reports, second, two harmless rules were not harmless together. Rule 3 styles the rows, and its :has() condition remains unchanged throughout the test. On its own, it costs nothing measurable. Put it in the same stylesheet as the second rule instead, and every toggle restyles all 5,000 rows plus the toolbar. That is about what it costs a script to restyle every row on purpose.

According to recent reports, let’s keep this in proportion. Since 7ms still fits inside a frame, nobody would notice it on this page. However, the browser is now restyling 5,001 elements to change just one, and neither rule says so. Also, the cost grows with the list. When I set the demo to 20,000 rows, the two rules together restyled 20,001 elements and took about 31ms per toggle, which is nearly two frames.

I can tell you what Chrome does here, but not why. Changing .is-selected on one row restyles every element that the other :has() rule targets, even though that rule never mentions .is-selected and its result never changes. I have filed this with the Chromium team as an matter, with a reduced test case, and I only tested Chrome. Whatever the cause, neither rule looks suspicious in a code review, and the cost applies only when both are met.

According to recent reports, that is system complexity in a single table. And please take the pattern from it, not the numbers: this is one page, one browser, and one machine.

The same goes for animation. The animation guide on web.dev recommends restricting animations to opacity and transform where possible, and warns that “an animation that moves an element using something other than transform is likely to be slow.” MDN’s CSS performance guide lists the properties that trigger layout when animated, such as width, height, margin, top, and left. A CSS transition on left runs layout on every frame, while a JavaScript animation of transform skips it. The property determines the cost, regardless of which language you write it in.

To be fair, CSS often wins. A script that reads layout, writes styles, and reads layout again forces the browser to do layout several times in one frame, and a container query hands that whole job to the browser. But that win is something you can measure, so measure it:.

Recent findings suggest that each of these scenarios is small on its own. The trouble is that a real migration could hit all four scenarios at once. You have already seen three of them. They are the three bugs in the “after” demo at the top of this article. Add a long list, and you get the fourth. One move-in, four housemates disturbed.

A team replaces a card’s JavaScript-driven responsive layout with a container query and :has(). The pull request adds twelve lines of CSS, deletes one script, and misses another. Within a month, three bug reports land, and there’s a chance a performance trace turns up as the fourth problem:.

None of these reports means that container queries or :has() were the wrong choice. Each bug lives in the meeting point between the new CSS and the system it moved into. Still, one small pull request has sent a developer through the JavaScript, the page layout, the cascade, and the profiler.

Sources indicate that and the way out is not a return to JavaScript. Here is the same page once more, fixed.

See the Pen [demo (fixed PR) [forked]](https://codepen.io/smashingmag/pen/wBJYpPJ) by Shoyombo Gabriel Ayomide.

It still uses a container query and :has(), with three changes:.

According to recent reports, this gap between a clean start and a real codebase shows up in the same r/webdev thread. The person who started it, JRM_Insights, opens with an observation that could describe any of our four scenarios:.

Further down, mq2thez describes moving an old CSS-in-JS codebase to a newer pattern: “In isolation or greenfield maybe it wouldn’t be a huge concern,” but in practice, it meant rewriting “whole component trees.” TheThirdRace, who had been defending the technology, answers that they had only ever evaluated it “from a greenfield project perspective,” and that it was “very enlightening to see this through the lens of a spaghetti CSS migration.”.

That is the honest version of this whole article.

Industry observers note that most of what we read about a upcoming feature is written from the greenfield perspective. Most of what we ship is a migration.

In a recent development, before you replace JavaScript with a modern CSS feature, or adopt one in an existing codebase, answer these six questions. Think of them as the conversation to have with the housemates before the latest tenant gets a key. I suggest putting the answers right in the pull request description.

In a recent development, modern CSS is great and a huge improvement to styling as a whole. In particular, container queries and :has() let us express things that used to need a script, a dependency, or a hack. But a latest capability does not hand us a simpler system by default. In every scenario we looked at, the new tenant did something that didn’t sit well with others, and that was because nobody introduced them to the housemates’ ways of doing things. We get a simpler system when the new rule has one clear owner, a scope we have checked, a place in the cascade we chose on purpose, and numbers showing it helped.

Recent findings suggest that so, the next time a pull request deletes more than it adds, enjoy the red lines. Then ask where the complexity went, and run the six questions. If you can’t answer one of them, the migration isn’t finished yet.

Healthcare company opens art gallery near Los Angeles

💡 Key Takeaways

  • AltaMed began collecting art in the 1970s, based on a belief that art is an integral part of holistic well-being.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AltaMed Health Services, a major healthcare provider in Southern California, is opening an art gallery, library and cultural centre to house its art collection in the Los Angeles suburb of Montebello. AltaMed’s collection, more than 50 years in the making, includes works by Laura Aguilar, Graciela Iturbide, Gabriel Orozco and others. Its upcoming 30,000-sq.-ft space, The Alta, opens to the public on Sunday (15 November).

AltaMed began collecting art in the 1970s, based on a belief that art is an integral part of holistic well-being. Since then, its collection has grown to some 4,000 pieces, with about 1,400 of them currently placed in its offices and clinics.

Sources indicate that “Our collection focuses on Chicano art," Cástulo de la Rocha, the president and chief executive of AltaMed (and founder of the collection), mentioned in a statement. "Because AltaMed was founded as part of the Chicano Movement in the 1970s, because I was active in the Chicano Movement, and because our patients and employees can connect culturally with the art.”.

In a recent development, in recent years, AltaMed has been converting a warehouse on the edge of a shopping mall in Montebello to house its collection. The space will have regular hours for visitors to tour its gallery, see works on shelves and sliding racks in open storage, and watch behind-the-scenes processes of digitisation and conservation. There is also studio space for artist residencies on site.

Patssi Valdez and rafa esparza’s Sacred and Profane Beauty (2026) Courtesy AltaMed.

Sources indicate that “The collection is here to serve the communities that AltaMed is focused on in Los Angeles and Orange County, primarily Latino communities,” Pilar Tompkins Rivas, AltaMed’s chief curator and vice president of arts, tells The Art Newspaper. “So we think about art that is relevant and celebratory of those populations.”.

Recent findings suggest that some recently acquired and commissioned works also address health and community—such as Sonia Romero’s mural The Fence-Pomona (2026), made expressly for the central communal space in a senior-care facility in nearby Pomona. The mural is 6ft high and 10ft wide, depicting a white lattice fence festooned with roses and the San Gabriel Mountains behind it. It ioverlooks a space used for meals, artmaking and gathering for patients.

AltaMed’s collection runs the gamut of media and spans more than 100 years, although most of the work was made after the Second World War. Early pieces include those of Hernando Gonzallo Villa, a commercial artist who famously designed ads and posters for the Santa Fe Railway. More recent works include drawings, prints and paintings by Carlos Almaraz, Judy Baca, Camille Rose Garcia, Gronk, Frank Romero, Eloy Torrez, John Valadez and Linda Vallejo.

The artist Felicia Montes at La Botánica del Barrio (2026) Courtesy AltaMed.

The first exhibition in the gallery is Patssi Valdez: LA LA LA (until 9 April 2027), featuring photo-based and collage works by a pioneer of Los Angeles’s Chicano art movement. For this show, Valdez re-created some of her photography from the 1970s and 80s—portraits of friends that helped define punk and goth glamour.

She indicates she had discussed doing something “out of the box” with AltaMed, and several of the framed work have coloured strips of paper flying out from the frame. To highlight some of her portraits, Valdez added Swarovski crystals to the prints, such as in Divine Dede (2026) and Hot Pink (Mario, Charlie & DeDe) (1983/2025). She also co-created work in collaboration with two younger artists, rafa esparza and Gabriela Ruiz.

In a recent development, it has been more than a decade since Valdez had a solo exhibition. “AltaMed has been a collector of my work for quite a while and has been very supportive," she says. The organization has purchased Valdez’s paintings and photography, and even one of her signature full-size paper dresses. One of these dresses is in a glass case in The Alta’s open-storage area.

Down the hall are the residency studios. The artist Rubén Esparza is working in one of them, where he has been making multimedia pieces featuring his "ongoing exploration of the cultural significance of Latinx, Chicano and Queer diasporas".

Recent findings suggest that the other studio has been transformed into an educational apothecary by Felicia Montes and her collective Mujeres de Maíz. La Botánica del Barrio (2026) features displays of samplable traditional herbal teas and tinctures, as well as a decorated pushcart. In the hallway, The Wellness Wall lets visitors put up cards with their own home remedies and healing practices. Visitors have suggested some very practical cures—from "talk to friends" and "travelling" to "Vicks" and "a good mezcal".

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that eric is a Boston-based designer who helps create straightforward solutions that address a person’s practical, physical, cognitive, and emotional needs. More about Eric ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

In a recent development, I have had the privilege of helping to improve the accessibility of multiple immersive LLM chat experiences in the course of my career. Now I want to share this knowledge with you.

Accessibility is a core part of a functional digital experience. As the LLM chat pattern continues to spread like wildfire across the web, we risk excluding people if these experiences are not built with accessibility as a core consideration.

It is also worth re-mentioning what “exclusion” means here: It’s the loss of knowledge, the loss of opportunity, the loss of utility, the loss of employability, the loss of entertainment, and more.

“Immersive LLM chat experience” is a catch-all term for full-screen experiences like Claude, ChatGPT, GitHub Copilot, Gemini, America.gov, Glean, and other similar websites and web apps:.

Industry observers note that the majority of what this post covers applies to both web apps and native apps. This is because these experiences are typically built using web technologies, then placed in a native wrapper via frameworks such as Electron or Tauri.

Industry observers note that immersive LLM chat experiences are not patterns such as a pop-up chat, inline text generation utilities, or summarization tools. These simpler applications of LLM technology will have different considerations and expectations. Instead, this is a starting point for making those other experiences accessible.

Industry observers note that there is nothing special about chat-based UIs when viewed via the lens of the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines. They are interactive experiences, built using web technologies. The losses I’ve described — and the legal liability associated with them — are access barriers in the same way any other web content can be an access barrier.

I would also like to mention the social model of disability here: the idea that exclusion can be created by the built environment. For example, consider an elevated entryway that uses a gently sloping ramp in place of stairs.

It has been revealed that built environments also extend to digital experiences, and the social model also applies here. The main activities undertaken to operate an LLM chat are already well-established:.

It is how we facilitate — or fail to facilitate — those interactions that’s the salient bit.

Before we get into the technical aspects, we must consider the overwhelming visual bias that permeates software creation.

Sources indicate that we live in a highly visual culture, so our outputs unconsciously reflect and reinforce that. What we need to do here is be aware of and think through the non-visual considerations.

While not all disabilities are blindness or low vision conditions, a lot of the core interactions of an LLM chat do need specific accommodations for these two types of disability.

In a recent development, recall the social model of disability here, and how it applies to the main flow of using an LLM-based chat. You:.

Let’s demonstrate at a high level what someone who can fully see the screen experiences compared to someone who uses a screen reader and cannot see the entire screen, or large portions of it:.

Recent findings suggest that visually, we can see the LLM reply appear. Someone who uses a screen reader does not know new content has appeared because:.

According to recent reports, so, how do we create an experience for someone who uses a screen reader that is equivalent to the experience of someone who can fully see the screen? To start, we use live regions.

It has been revealed that live region announcements will enable someone to know what the LLM has responded with without having to move focus from the input used for prompting. This is equivalent to someone who can see the screen, glancing upwards to read the LLM response when it appears.

First, read this excellent article by TetraLogical if this is your first attempt at getting live region announcements working. They’re tricky to get right, and this article sets the record straight.

Recent findings suggest that one common pitfall I want to call specific attention to is applying aria-live on each LLM response message. Don’t do this. Instead, use a dedicated live region area to announce each message’s content.

It has been revealed that the live region area should be placed at the end of the DOM and used for all live region messaging. This method is far more stable and reliable, which is key for ensuring everyone understands what the experience is communicating.

With that established: What we want to do is trigger a live region announcement when the LLM’s chat reply shows up in full on the screen.

This creates an outcome where you can read the message if you can see the screen, and hear or feel the message if you cannot.

Recent findings suggest that there are a few things to do when creating a good user experience for the people who rely on these live region announcements. These considerations mean the difference between a compliant-yet-unusable outcome and something that genuinely works for the person using it.

Attempting to announce the message as it streams in may create a juddering and confusing experience that’s difficult for someone to parse.

It is better to wait until the message has completed streaming, and then announce the message’s content in full.

It has been revealed that responses from an LLM often take time to complete. Generally speaking, there are three ways to show a response is still processing:.

Sources indicate that these experiences are typically only shown visually. If you cannot see the screen, it may lead to it feeling like the experience has stalled or crashed — especially if the response is for a large or complicated request that takes a while to work through.

To address this, we’ll want to use live region announcements:.

Recent findings suggest that if text is visually shown on the screen: Ensure a companion live region announcement is also triggered at the same time the loading message text is displayed. The text string for the live region announcement should be the same as what is shown visually, to be sure to ensure parity of experience:.

If a text-less loading animation is shown on the screen: Ensure the loading state is also communicated to assistive technology.

It has been revealed that A live region announcement that mentions the reply is loading after a set amount of time will facilitate an equivalent experience for this interaction. It doesn’t have to be too verbose; the word “Loading” can suffice:.

Triggering the loading message five seconds after prompt submission seems to be the sweet spot, according to the inclusive user research I evaluated. You can then have your logic repeat the loading message every five seconds until the LLM completes its actual reply.

It has been revealed that be sure to also announce the reply immediately as it finishes streaming. You don’t need to wait until the next five-second loading message cycle is complete.

Also consider randomly selecting from a set of different phrases that communicate that a response is being formulated after the initial “Loading” message is dispatched. This helps in scenarios where someone may think the loading experience itself has crashed or stalled.

We’ll eventually be able to replace the technique TetraLogical outlined with ariaNotify(). It is a much-needed and welcome addition to the platform, and will drastically lower the hacks and headaches many developers encounter when creating and managing live region announcements.

Baseline lists the ariaNotify() method as having cross-browser availability at the time of this article’s publication. However, there are two factors to consider here:.

Also consider that while a polyfill for ariaNotify() is available, you need to factor in whether it has both:.

What this realistically means is holding off for a while on ariaNotify() in favor of the tried and true TetraLogical live region technique.

Headings are the most popular way people who use screen readers navigate around an experience. Because of this, I advocate for inserting visually-hidden headings before each chat message.

Here’s a simplified version of that in code:.

And here’s what the code might look like using the actual content from a human question and an LLM response:.

So, why the “You stated:”/”Cody said:” prefix? Remember the visual bias. Visually, we can see the left- or right-hand alignment of messages, used to indicate who is saying what.

The prefix serves the same purpose: identifying the message’s owner. This allows people to swiftly move through a conversation the same way someone might quickly scroll upwards to re-establish context, checking who said what and when.

Using landmark regions to wrap the larger overall areas of your LLM chat experience helps people understand its overall layout. It can also enable quick screen reader navigation to each area:.

Landmarks allow someone who cannot see the screen to learn about its overall makeup. This is the equivalent of how we swiftly move our eyes and tilt our heads to different overall areas when scanning the screen to initially learn the overall layout of an experience.

I am hesitant to wrap chat messages in section or other landmark elements. The reason for this is that they “pollute” the list of landmarks a screen reader can generate, making navigation more laborious. This is especially relevant for long-running sessions where many messages are present.

Compare the following and ask yourself which one would be easier to move through with your keyboard if trying to jump from the prompt content area back to the sessions area:.

Here, our visually hidden heading elements serve as a dedicated navigation mechanism for moving through the LLM conversation.

In addition to headings and landmarks, there are two other ways to let people get around quickly:.

Skip links — sometimes referred to as skip navigation — allow you to rapidly jump to another area on the same page or view.

Skip to main content links are commonplace on many mature websites and web apps. Immersive LLM chat experiences should be no different.

Place a skip link in the DOM that allows someone to jump to the main conversation area before any other DOM content that is shown visually on the screen.

Also consider using additional skip links that enable:.

Composite widgets are used when a discrete section of content contains multiple interactive elements. Focus is then managed within this section by the developer, so that:.

For the purposes of an immersive LLM chat experience, we want to make conversation lists composite widgets. This enables someone to quickly navigate both within and past the entire list.

It has been revealed that here, consider the use case of someone who exclusively relies on a keyboard to navigate. Compare pressing Tab 50 times to get through each of the 50 conversation sessions you’ve created versus pressing Tab once. Now consider motor control conditions where those keypresses can be fatiguing, or even painful to perform.

Once someone places focus on a conversation list composite widget, they can use the Up and Down arrow keys to navigate through each conversation session list item.

As a quality-of-life improvement, I also like to support the following keyboard interactions:.

To save you a lot of headaches and prototyping: Corner cases around focus management and usability expectations for people who rely exclusively on keyboards work against you if you try to go with a feed pattern approach.

Recent findings suggest that there’s no need to unnecessarily overcomplicate things. The article elements’ wrapping messages with visually-hidden headings approach that I’ve described earlier is both simple and effective.

Industry observers note that people who use assistive technology understand the simpler approach, and it involves far less effort to maintain. It’s a win-win!

Pressing F6/Shift+F6 to hop around different areas of the app is an older navigation technique some people who use Windows screen readers employ when navigating through installable desktop apps. Think of it a lot like navigating by landmark.

Sources indicate that LLM chat experiences are effectively apps in their own right. Because of this, we can recreate the F6 navigation experience and accommodate those who might attempt it. That means:.

In a recent development, there’s no secret sauce here. For starters, place an id on each landmark, as well as tabindex="-1". Also ensure each landmark other than main has an accessible name, granted via either aria-label or aria-labelledby.

After that, have an event listener set up to recognize Control+F6 and Control+Shift+F6 key presses. Set focus to:.

In a recent development, and voilà! We now have web-based F6 navigation.

As it is an older technique, people who are younger or less experienced with screen readers may not know F6 navigation exists.

Recent findings suggest that consider socializing the capability in the accessibility portion of your application’s settings menu to address this lack of awareness. Also consider exposing and making F6 navigation re-bindable as another discovery technique, provided your application supports keyboard shortcut rebinding.

Again, this advice only applies to an immersive LLM chat experience. Help agent popups and other less-sophisticated experiences have different expectations.

There are two areas that deserve more finesse when considering where to set focus when F6 navigation is used: the prompting input and the conversation.

Setting focus directly on the input used to type prompts — and not its parent form landmark element — allows someone to rapidly get into the action.

Similarly, setting focus on the visually hidden heading of the last message displayed allows them to promptly jump to the content the LLM generated — a data attribute such as data-last-message can be really helpful for managing this.

Using F6 and Shift+F6 keypresses allows someone to hop from the chat input to what the LLM outputs, then back again. This enables rapid keyboard-based review and iteration on an LLM’s output.

Adjust the text size of your experience and double-check that content is not clipped, or that there’s horizontal overflow.

It has been revealed that people increase the text size of the experiences they use, and more than you’d probably guess. They also resize application windows. Also consider that most LLM-based chat designs tend to use a smaller text size to allow for more information shown on screen.

Because of these two factors, it makes sense to evaluate how your experience holds up when the browser font size is increased.

Customization lives at the heart of accessibility. It’s only natural that LLM-based chat experiences have preferences to better accommodate all the different ways people use them.

In that vein, thoughtful preference offerings can go a long way to helping out people with access needs. Here are some that I’ve found to be particularly useful.

According to recent reports, some LLMs perform interim actions that are circumstantially less crucial than the messages they ultimately generate. Here, consider programming-oriented LLMs. They can perform actions like researching and reasoning, code search, and tool calls.

These secondary actions typically have a smaller, less visually vital treatment compared to the messages that contain the main LLM response content. This is because the results are more important than the methodology when using this type of interaction.

Announcing each of these secondary actions could lead to a confusing or overwhelming experience, especially if multiple actions are clustered and fire off live messages in rapid succession.

Recent findings suggest that to address this, you can allow people to circumstantially switch off the announcements for this type of ancillary information. The content in the conversation is still present; it just isn’t announced via a live region. This is equivalent to how someone who can see the screen can skim over them.

Letting someone re-enable these types of announcements also grants parity in experience, in that it allows them to know the actions are happening if they want a more information-intensive experience. This is equivalent to someone who can see the screen, intentionally paying close attention to the LLM’s actions.

Sources indicate that it might also be worth investigating letting people toggle visually hiding and showing these less vital announcements, as well. This can help people with attention or cognitive considerations, who may be less familiar with technical jargon.

According to recent reports, loading animations and large animated effects, like streaming conversations and side panels expanding and collapsing, can be distracting for some people with attention and cognitive considerations. That can go a long way toward breaking someone’s flow.

To address this, you can provide a toggle to turn off animations, reducing their transition time to zero.

You should also strive to be a respectful and courteous steward of the experience. Default your animation toggle to an off state if a request for a reduced motion experience has been in the device operating system. You can use the prefers-reduced-motion media feature to achieve this. Also consider a setting that can re-enable animation, even if a reduced motion request is present.

Some people can get distracted by, or have their focus disrupted by, sound effects. This is similar to animation considerations.

Letting people turn off app-specific sound effects means they don’t have to mute their entire device. Here, consider things like other apps playing flow state-inducing music or white noise that they might be using to help them focus.

Alternatives for sound-based notifications include, but are not limited to:.

I am of the school of thought that any experience that uses keyboard shortcuts also needs to allow both editing and being switched off, both in bulk and on a shortcut-by-shortcut basis.

You may be quick to think of conflicts with assistive technology, but I’d also like to take this space to remind you of different language keyboard layouts.

Live region messages are plain text strings. These strings are confirmed by screen readers in full in one go from start to end.

It has been revealed that semantic information that comes for free by using the appropriate HTML element isn’t present in live region announcements—it’s stripped out. Because of that, we need to think about how we could make our live region content both clear and useful.

Each type of special content has its own considerations. For my work, I created special cases for tables and blocks of code:.

In a recent development, A table’s cell content will sound odd when confirmed without the companion semantic structure conferred by elements such as table, th, tr, and td. Relationships between columns and rows aren’t present in a live region announcement, either.

Because of this, we can convert the live region announcement of tables to use a concise description of the number of rows and columns, plus a general description and overall trends it might highlight.

A block of code sounds like gibberish when the line breaks are stripped away, and the content is flattened into a single string.

And if it’s a large block of code, it can be a tedious amount of gibberish to parse — nobody wants to sit through an announcement of 2,376 lines of code, painstakingly declared character-by-character.

To accommodate this, we can convert the live region announcement of code blocks to use the filename or file type, plus how many lines of code the block contains.

Also note here that people can revisit the actual message content itself. The actual message content will ideally have the appropriate semantics applied to it. This means things like tables being announced as, and navigated through as, table content.

Recent findings suggest that in this way, the live region message is a context-setting preview of what to expect. This is the equivalent of quickly visually skimming a message as it is streaming in, then scrolling back to review its content with more attention afterward.

Industry observers note that all of the previous is built atop feedback from testing different approaches and noting what works, and what could be improved. You want to facilitate disabled people being the experts in their own lived experience, and not treat others’ advice as the more credible source.

Industry observers note that inclusive user research is a vital way of determining if an experience is actually usable. Centering disabled people’s observations and perspectives is a way to take an experience beyond baseline compliance and create something usable and equitable.

It is vital to ensure that everyone can use chat-based LLM interactions as the pattern continues to proliferate. Although this is not an exhaustive list of everything you’ll need to do, the content above covers a wide swath of the main places accessibility barriers and friction may show up.

It is my sincerest hope that the improvements I’ve learned about and implemented can help you with your efforts to make chat-based experiences on the web more accessible and usable for people who use assistive technology to get what they want or need online.

Thank you to Sarah Higley, whose research and efforts in this area informed key parts of this work.

Should You Actually Add AI To That? A Four-Question Audit For Product Teams
