Tech Report: Frieze Artist Award reimagines endangered Lebanese site

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (416 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that one of Lebanon’s most intriguing archaeological sites is the inspiration behind the inaugural Frieze Abu Dhabi Artist Award, given to the fast-rising Lebanese artist Dala Nasser to create her installation Qubbat Duris.
  • Placed in the atrium of the fair, the work will comprise a timber frame evoking Qubbat Duris’s structure, with fabrics covered in charcoal rubbings of the remaining ruins and painted with ash, raw clay and terracotta draped over it.
  • Nasser is best known for her archaeological frottage paintings—made using the surfaces of endangered historical sites—which consider the artist’s role in reproducing, and bearing witness to, history and landscape.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that one of Lebanon’s most intriguing archaeological sites is the inspiration behind the inaugural Frieze Abu Dhabi Artist Award, given to the fast-rising Lebanese artist Dala Nasser to create her installation Qubbat Duris. The work takes its name from a 13th-century Muslim shrine near Baalbek, northeast of Beirut, which is composed from the ruins of two separate ancient Roman sites: granite columns from Baalbek’s Temple of Jupiter hold up limestone sarcophagi from a necropolis.

Placed in the atrium of the fair, the work will comprise a timber frame evoking Qubbat Duris’s structure, with fabrics covered in charcoal rubbings of the remaining ruins and painted with ash, raw clay and terracotta draped over it.

Nasser is best known for her archaeological frottage paintings—made using the surfaces of endangered historical sites—which consider the artist’s role in reproducing, and bearing witness to, history and landscape.

Though Nasser is not the first artist to engage with Qubbat Duris, she points out, many of her antecedents are problematic. “The site has already been extensively imagined and reimagined in art historical painting,” she tells The Art Newspaper. “From Orientalist depictions to the backdrop to one of Gertrude Bell’s most circulated photographs, taken in costume on horseback.”.

In a recent development, similar works of Nasser’s—such as Adonis River (2023) and Wedding at Qana (2024)—have also taken as their subjects “landscapes that loom large in historical painting but look nothing like the landscape itself in Western Asia, either overwhelmed by Orientalist tropes or painted as scenes of European countryside, betraying the artists’ lack of knowledge and limits of imagination”, she claims. “I am trying to make paintings that are truthful to the landscape.”.

The question of “truth” pertains to Qubbat Duris’s position as a site that reflects the layered cultural histories and religions of Lebanon. “It exists as a palimpsest from the second century AD until today, carrying all of the traces in between,” Nasser notes.

Meanwhile, the role of evidence and recording in Nasser’s practice also considers the risks of erasure faced by much of Lebanon’s cultural artefacts, particularly from Israel’s longstanding and continued occupation of the country. On 15 October 2024, Qubbat Duris sustained slight damage from Israeli airstrikes; previously during the 2006 Israel-Lebanon war, an Israeli airstrike dislodged one of the shrine’s stones. “I’m interested in how a place like Qubbat Duris carries physical evidence of everything it’s endured, including scars of damage,” Nasser indicates.

• Frieze Abu Dhabi, Manarat Al Saadiyat, 19-22 November.

Pablo Castillo partners with Decibel on 3D-printed chair with under-seat storage

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (352 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A bookshelf slots in below the cantilevered seat of Kino, a 3D-printed chair developed by Barcelona-based designer Pablo Castillo.
  • According to recent reports, castillo designed Kino for Decibel, an American firm that specialises in 3D-printed furniture and installations.
  • The designer’s aim was to create a recognisable chair silhouette, while also responding to the specificities of the 3D printing process.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A bookshelf slots in below the cantilevered seat of Kino, a 3D-printed chair developed by Barcelona-based designer Pablo Castillo.

According to recent reports, castillo designed Kino for Decibel, an American firm that specialises in 3D-printed furniture and installations. It is shortlisted for seating design of the year in the upcoming Dezeen Awards.

The designer’s aim was to create a recognisable chair silhouette, while also responding to the specificities of the 3D printing process.

The chair is essentially a monobloc, with a single component forming the T-shaped seat, two legs, the shelf and a curved backrest.

Its entire form is printed from PLA, the most common bioplastic, although the material is reinforced with cellulose plant fibres. This increases its strength, enabling the cantilevered seat.

Decibal also offers an outdoor version printed from recycled PETG, a thermoplastic polyester.

“I wanted the substantial thickness of the plastic and the way it builds a product layer by layer to translate into features that give the chair its character,” Castillo told Dezeen.

“Following this line of thought allowed me to move beyond mere dimensions and general ergonomic considerations,” the designer said.

“The cantilevered seat, the under-seat storage, and specific details such as the T-junctions naturally emerged.”.

The seat’s T-shape was created by cantilevers both forwards and backwards. This makes the chair less rigid than a typical 3D-printed chair, improving comfort.

“By reinforcing the lower part of the seat with a corrugated structure integrated directly into the 3D print, we achieved a chair that offers a slightly broader range of motion than a traditional design,” Castillo mentioned.

“It seamlessly accommodates highly reclined, relaxed postures, as well as more active positions when the user leans forward.”.

Kino joins Decibel’s Editions collection, which also includes chairs by designers including Charles Birshaw, Karim Rashid and Deniz Aktay.

The New Jersey-based brand launched this collection with an exhibition at the Alcova show in Milan in 2025, when it was live-printing chairs in the former SNIA factory in Varedo.

The chairs are produced using a Caracol robotic 3D printer, which allows geometries that wouldn’t be possible with injection moulding.

#33850. Virgin Atlantic → Delta One Suites

📅 03 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 16m • 📚 Deep Dive (3138 w)

Virgin Atlantic → Delta One Suites

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3138 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Choosefi

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.
  • The best workaround for Delta dynamic pricing on premium cabins.
  • Picture this: you're settling into a private suite at 35,000 feet somewhere over the American heartland.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

The best workaround for Delta dynamic pricing on premium cabins.

Picture this: you're settling into a private suite at 35,000 feet somewhere over the American heartland. The door clicks shut. There's a full-flat bed, a sliding privacy door, a personal minibar, and a cabin crew member who just handed you a glass of something sparkling before you've even thought to ask. This is Delta One Suites on the Airbus A350-900 — one of the best domestic business class products flying today — and you're on your way from New York to Los Angeles for 50,000 Virgin Atlantic Flying Club miles. Let that sink in for a moment. The same seat on the same flight regularly retails for **$2,500 to $6,000 in cash**. At the low end of that range, your 50,000 points are delivering **5 cents per point (CPP)**. At the high end — during peak travel seasons or last-minute premium bookings — you're looking at **12 cents per point**. For context, most travel rewards programs consider 1–2 CPP a "good" redemption. You're potentially doing six times better than that. The ChooseFI community is built on a foundational principle: the gap between what something *costs* and what you *pay* is where wealth is built. That principle applies to points redemptions just as powerfully as it applies to index fund expense ratios. When the market (Delta's dynamic pricing engine) says $4,000 and your award chart says 50,000 points, you've just found a pricing inefficiency — and exploiting it intelligently is exactly what savvy travel rewards strategy is all about. What makes this redemption especially compelling is the *product*. Delta One Suites on the A350-900 isn't a legacy business class seat in name only. The sliding door gives you genuine privacy. The fully flat bed means you arrive in LA rested instead of stiff. The suite design is genuinely luxurious — the kind of experience that, for most people, lives permanently in the "someday, maybe" category. Travel rewards exist to move that experience from "someday" to your actual calendar. For a couple traveling together, this redemption scales elegantly: 100,000 points gets two people into private suites on one of America's most competitive premium routes. That's a combined retail value potentially north of $10,000 — for points you may have earned simply by paying your regular monthly expenses on the right credit cards. This is what the system looks like when it works.

It has been revealed that here's the insight that changes everything: Delta prices its own award seats dynamically, which means when you search Delta.com for a SkyMiles redemption, you're at the mercy of an algorithm that reads demand, load factors, and booking timing. A Delta One Suite that costs 50,000 SkyMiles one week might jump to 120,000 or even 250,000 SkyMiles the next. It's unpredictable, often punishing, and fundamentally unfair to the loyal customer who saved up miles expecting consistency.

Virgin Atlantic Flying Club doesn't play by those rules.

Virgin Atlantic is a Delta SkyTeam partner, which means Flying Club members can book seats on Delta-operated flights using their Virgin Atlantic miles. But critically — and this is the entire mechanism — Virgin Atlantic prices Delta award seats on a fixed award chart, not Delta's dynamic pricing system. That chart presently prices Delta One (business class) on transcon routes like JFK–LAX at 50,000 miles one-way. No matter what Delta's algorithm is doing that day, your Virgin Atlantic redemption rate stays fixed.

It has been revealed that this is a classic pricing inefficiency created by partner award charts lagging behind airline pricing strategies. Delta has every incentive to raise its own SkyMiles pricing — it captures more revenue from its own loyalty currency. But Delta has far less control over what a partner program charges to access its seats. Virgin Atlantic's award chart is, in effect, a door into Delta inventory that bypasses Delta's own toll booth.

The points you need to fund this redemption are almost certainly already sitting in currencies you have or can easily earn:.

Sources indicate that for a redemption this valuable, the 1:1 instant transfers from Chase, Amex, Citi, and Bilt are your primary path. You transfer exactly what you need, the miles appear in your Flying Club account immediately, and you book. No waiting, no uncertainty.

In a recent development, virgin Atlantic has a reputation for imposing high fuel surcharges on its own operated flights — and that reputation is well-earned. But here's the critical nuance: surcharges do NOT apply to partner awards. When you book a Delta-operated flight through Virgin Atlantic Flying Club, you pay only the standard carrier-imposed taxes and fees, which are minimal on domestic U.S. routes. On JFK–LAX, expect to pay roughly $5–$15 in taxes. That's it. The surcharge concern that makes some people avoid Virgin Atlantic entirely simply doesn't apply here.

Flying Club miles expire after 36 months of account inactivity. Keep your account active with at least one earning or redemption activity every three years, and your miles will remain intact indefinitely. This is a very traveler-friendly policy compared to programs with hard expiration dates.

Do NOT start at Virgin Atlantic's website — their search tool for partner awards is limited. Instead, go directly to delta.com and search for your desired route (e.g., JFK → LAX) in the date range you're targeting. Select "Use miles" as your payment method and filter by Business class. You're not booking here — you're prospecting.

Industry observers note that what you're looking for: Delta One availability showing in the results. When you see it, note the exact flight number, date, and departure time. Delta.com will show you the SkyMiles price (which will be high under dynamic pricing), but ignore that number entirely. You just need to confirm the seat exists.

You need 50,000 Virgin Atlantic Flying Club miles per person. Before transferring anything, confirm which flexible points currency you're working with:.

Industry observers note that all transfer at 1:1 instantly. If you're using Marriott Bonvoy points, the ratio is 3:1 (so 150,000 Bonvoy points = 50,000 Flying Club miles), and transfers take 1–5 days.

Once you've confirmed availability on a specific flight, transfer your points. Use the transfer portal within your credit card program's website (Chase, Amex, Citi, or Bilt). You'll need your Flying Club membership number — create a free account at virginatlantic.com/us/en/flying-club if you don't have one.

In a recent development, for Chase, Amex, Citi, and Bilt transfers: miles appear instantly in your Flying Club account. Confirm the balance before proceeding.

Critical warning: Do not transfer points until you've verbally confirmed availability with a Virgin Atlantic agent (Step 4). Points transfers are irreversible.

Recent findings suggest that this is a phone booking, not an online booking. Call Virgin Atlantic Flying Club at 1-800-365-9500. Have your flight details ready:.

Ask the agent to confirm that Delta One award availability exists on your chosen flight before you transfer points. If they confirm it, then transfer and call back — or ask to be placed on a brief hold while you complete the transfer (instant transfers make this possible).

Once your miles are transferred and the agent has confirmed availability, they'll complete the booking. You'll pay only standard carrier taxes and fees — expect roughly $5–$15 for a domestic U.S. route. You'll receive a Virgin Atlantic booking confirmation, but your ticket will show Delta as the operating carrier.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Giant comets blaze across dark skies, volcanoes rain down fire on hapless cities, floods rage and the moon turns blood red in a spectacular 16th-century manuscript coming up for auction at Christie’s in London, estimated between £700,000 and £1m.

The Book of Miracles, with 167 vivid watercolours illustrating natural phenomena—real and imagined—and scenes from the Old and Latest Testaments, was completed in Augsburg, Germany, around 1552. It is attributed to Hans Burgkmair the Younger and Heinrich Vogtherr the Younger, painters, print makers and designers who had separate workshops but sometimes collaborated on crucial commissions.

A page from the The Book of Miracles (around 1552) CHRISTIE'S IMAGES LTD. 2026.

Eugenio Donadoni, the director and international specialist in Medieval and Renaissance manuscripts at Christie’s, called the book an exquisite work, with its illustrations as vibrant after nearly 500 years as the day they were made. “Beyond their extraordinary beauty, these images offer us a glimpse into how people in the 16th century made sense of a world that could often seem mysterious and unpredictable. Today, we might understand a comet, an eclipse or an earthquake through science, but in the Renaissance these phenomena could be interpreted as signs of something greater, even as warnings of what was to come,” he states. “The manuscript brings together the remarkable visual imagination of the period, the events that captured people's attention and provoked their wonder and fear. Nearly 500 years later, these images remain as compelling as ever.”.

According to recent reports, A page from the The Book of Miracles (around 1552) CHRISTIE'S IMAGES LTD. 2026.

According to recent reports, the book is included in a series of sales of works from the Mickey Cartin collection. Cartin, who is based in Connecticut and built the electrical supply firm founded by his grandfather into a national company, began collecting in the 1980s across many categories, including books and manuscripts, old master paintings, furniture and contemporary art. Artnews included in him in its Top 200 Collectors list every year from 2007-13. He bought The Book of Miracles in 2010, three years after it was rediscovered in a private collection in Bavaria, and it acquired wider fame when the art publisher Taschen published a facsimile edition in 2013.

The manuscript, part of the sale An Alchemy of Ideas: Works from the Mickey Cartin Collection, will be on public view at Christie’s King Street sales room in London on 4-10 December, before the sale on 10 December.

One month after launch, MaPC has shipped 32 versions, added three stores, and run The Witcher 3 and Hogwarts Legacy on Mac.

It has been revealed that maPC released in mid-October as a free native Mac app that runs Windows games from Steam, Epic Games and GOG on Apple Silicon, with no Wine setup and no tinkering. Connect a store account, install a game, press Play. DirectX 9, 10 and 11 run through Wine, DXVK and MoltenVK, all set up automatically, with per-game graphics settings, Retina rendering and a performance HUD. The interface takes its colors from each game's cover art, and the library switches between a Magazine view and a Panels view.

In a recent development, the pace since launch has been fast. MaPC is now on version 1.1.32, with 32 releases in the 1.1 line alone. Four of them landed on a single day this week, mostly fixes for Red Dead Redemption 2 and the Rockstar Launcher. Three more stores joined during the month: Amazon Games, the EA app and Ubisoft Connect. Epic cloud saves arrived too, along with controller fixes and a help page for games that may run.

Industry observers note that the response has been the best part. The launch post passed 1,100 likes and 100 replies on Threads, and the game posts kept going: 007 First Light passed 1,200 likes, Hogwarts Legacy passed 700, The Witcher 3 passed 400. The games people played say it well: Guardians of the Galaxy, Red Dead Redemption 2, Batman Arkham Knight, Jedi Fallen Order, Kena, Winds of Viridia, Pragmata, and free demos of Onimusha and Resident Evil Requiem.

Two of the runs are on video: 44 seconds of Batman: Arkham Knight, and Red Dead Redemption 2 at 60 fps.

We will keep improving it, because we at Abduzeedo love to play games and we love our Mac. MaPC is free in public beta for Apple Silicon Macs on macOS 15 and up. Find it at mapc.games, with the full changelog there.

#33842. Has the couple in Jan van Eyck’s ‘Arnolfini Portrait’ been misidentified?

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1007 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theartnewspaper ↗ Open Full Page

Has the couple in Jan van Eyck’s ‘Arnolfini Portrait’ been misidentified?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1007 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Jan van Eyck’s Arnolfini Portrait (1434) has been a signature work in London’s National Gallery since it arrived at the museum in 1842.
  • Now, on the occasion of the National Gallery’s exhibition Van Eyck: The Portraits (21 November-11 April 2027), which brings together all nine of the artist’s surviving panel portraits, the Berlin-based curator Stephan Kemperdick, writing in a catalogue essay, has planted a possible bombshell by suggesting that the man in the Arnolfini Portrait is Van Eyck himself, and that the woman standing next to him is the artist’s wife Margaret, the sitter in another Van Eyck portrait from 1439, which is on loan to the show from Bruges.
  • Sources indicate that kemperdick’s theory, presented in recent talks but published now for the first time, is not an entirely newly introduced one.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jan van Eyck’s Arnolfini Portrait (1434) has been a signature work in London’s National Gallery since it arrived at the museum in 1842. A few key facts about the dual portrait, showing a youngish man and his idealised wife, could be gleaned just by looking at the work’s prominent Latin inscription, which translates as “Jan van Eyck was here 1434”. Over the years, just about everything else associated with the painting, from its mysterious room to the obscure occasion, has been open to debate, other than the surname of the man—Arnolfini, connected to an extended family of wealthy merchants from Lucca active in 15th-century Bruges, where Van Eyck had his studio.

Now, on the occasion of the National Gallery’s exhibition Van Eyck: The Portraits (21 November-11 April 2027), which brings together all nine of the artist’s surviving panel portraits, the Berlin-based curator Stephan Kemperdick, writing in a catalogue essay, has planted a possible bombshell by suggesting that the man in the Arnolfini Portrait is Van Eyck himself, and that the woman standing next to him is the artist’s wife Margaret, the sitter in another Van Eyck portrait from 1439, which is on loan to the show from Bruges.

Sources indicate that kemperdick’s theory, presented in recent talks but published now for the first time, is not an entirely newly introduced one. In the late 1840s, the National Gallery’s future first director Charles Eastlake contended that the artist’s inscription, which he thought could be translated as “Jan van Eyck was this [one]”, meant that the painting was also a dual portrait of the artist and his wife. But in the early 1860s, the British art historian W. H. James Weale interpreted a reference in a 16th-century inventory to a certain “hernoul le fin” in the painting, which he regarded as the French version of the Italian surname Arnolfini. The connection between the couple and that family was thus set in stone, though scholars disagree, often vehemently, about which particular member of the Arnolfini clan is shown.

Kemperdick has revisited the inscription, which is unusually large and conspicuously places the artist’s name next to the male figure’s head. He argues this indicates a direct connection between Van Eyck and the man. He has also reconsidered the association between the “hernoul le fin” reference and the surname Arnolfini. Citing the early-modern categorisation of the late-medieval work as not a portrait at all, but rather a lewd genre painting, Kemperdick suggests that “hernoul le fin” is not the correct surname of the sitter, but a subsequent and mocking moniker used by later generations to misidentify the man as a “a deceived cheat”. Kemperdick also suggests that a reference to St Margaret in the bedstead statue near the woman’s head serves to identify her as Van Eyck’s wife.

It has been revealed that kemperdick is the curator of German, Netherlandish and French Paintings before 1600 at the Berlin Gemäldegalerie, which is noted for its Early Netherlandish holdings and has in its own collection a Van Eyck portrait (around 1435-38) of the very same man who appears in the National Gallery’s Arnolfini Portrait. The two will be shown together in the London exhibition.

Nicholas Flory, the co-curator of Van Eyck: The Portraits along with Emma Capron, the National Gallery’s curator of early Netherlandish and German painting, says that he and Capron find Kemperdick’s theory “interesting” but “speculative”, citing, among other reasons, that the woman in the Bruges portrait, whom we know to be Margaret based on the inscription, has greyish-blue eyes while the woman in the Arnolfini Portrait has brown eyes.

In a recent development, other leading Van Eyck scholars also have their doubts. The German art historian Till-Holger Borchert—now the director of the Suermondt-Ludwig-Museum in Aachen and the former director of Musea Brugge in Bruges—is familiar with Kemperdick’s theory. “I’m not entirely sure I can concur,” he notes. He thinks the early-16th-century inventory reference—associated with the painting’s owner at the time, Margaret of Austria, the governor of the Habsburg Netherlands—is a near iron-clad reference to the Arnolfinis. The Ghent University art historian Maximiliaan Martens, who has been involved in the lengthy restoration of Van Eyck’s Ghent Altarpiece, also “doesn’t see any reason to doubt” that the inventory reference is to the Arnolfinis.

Industry observers note that the implications of Kemperdick’s theory are far-reaching. Another Van Eyck portrait at the National Gallery, from 1433, showing a much older man than the figure in the Arnolfini Portrait, is now tentatively identified by the London museum as a self-portrait. This, however, cannot be the case if Kemperdick’s theory is correct.

Industry observers note that the exhibition Van Eyck: The Portraits will label the Berlin work with its previous and longstanding reference to the Arnolfinis, while the Gemäldegalerie, under Kemperick’s guidance, has recently renamed it Portrait of a Man with a Red Chaperon. And the debate about the couple promises to continue long after the show closes in April.

Sources indicate that “I have thought for 30 years about this,” Martens says of the figures in the Arnolfini Portrait. He says he is still not sure if the man is Giovanni di Arrigo Arnolfini (who was apparently not married at the time the painting was made) or his cousin, Giovanni di Nicolao Arnolfini (whose wife had died before the painting was made).

Other aspects of the dual portrait that scholars continue to debate include whether the heavy-bellied woman is actually pregnant (Kemperdick and Martens think that may be possible, while Flory and Capron think she is just gathering up her heavy skirts), and whether the room itself is a real space or an imagined one (imagined, say Flory and Capron; real, claims Martens).

Sources indicate that beyond who made it and when, the Arnolfini Portrait remains a mystery, which is in keeping for an artist whose date and place of birth, among other foundational knowledge, is also speculation. Asked to comment on the enigma associated with the Arnolfini Portrait, Borchert claims: “Can you tell me anything about Van Eyck that isn’t enigmatic?”.

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (843 w)

Show of every Jan van Eyck portrait reveals many newly introduced sides to his works

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (843 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that there is a lot we do not know for certain about Jan van Eyck, including where and when he was born.
  • According to recent reports, but we stand to know a lot more about him this month, when London’s National Gallery brings together all nine of his surviving panel portraits along with his lone surviving drawing, also a portrait.
  • Fresh from a conservation treatment completed in 2024, the National Gallery’s own Portrait of a Man (Self-Portrait?) (1433) will meet up with Portrait of Margaret van Eyck (1439), the artist’s wife, on loan from Bruges, where Van Eyck had his workshop when he was the court painter to Philip the Good, Duke of Burgundy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that there is a lot we do not know for certain about Jan van Eyck, including where and when he was born. What we do know is that his career—from the early 1420s until his death in 1441—helped launch the Early Netherlandish school, influencing the use of oil paint far beyond his native Low Countries and instilling a fresh and arguably everlasting value of verisimilitude in Western art.

According to recent reports, but we stand to know a lot more about him this month, when London’s National Gallery brings together all nine of his surviving panel portraits along with his lone surviving drawing, also a portrait. The bijoux blockbuster show will give scholars a unique opportunity to compare scattered works of singular importance. Van Eyck: The Portraits—with a checklist that expands all the way to 13 through the addition of three works on paper by his followers—is built around some remarkable pairings.

Fresh from a conservation treatment completed in 2024, the National Gallery’s own Portrait of a Man (Self-Portrait?) (1433) will meet up with Portrait of Margaret van Eyck (1439), the artist’s wife, on loan from Bruges, where Van Eyck had his workshop when he was the court painter to Philip the Good, Duke of Burgundy.

The National Gallery’s Arnolfini Portrait (1434), Van Eyck’s enigmatic view of an elegantly dressed couple in an impressive reception room, will be shown for the first time with its related work from the Gemäldegalerie in Berlin clearly showing the same man, Portrait of a Man (Giovanni Arnolfini?) (around 1435-38).

Vienna’s Kunsthistorisches Museum is loaning Portrait of an Elderly Man (A Scholar?) (around 1438). It will be shown with the preparatory drawing from Dresden, in goldpoint and silverpoint on prepared paper, with its revealing notes on how to colour the painting itself.

Van Eyck’s devotional portraits, such as those in his groundbreaking Ghent Altarpiece and the Musée du Louvre’s recently treated Madonna of Chancellor Rolin (around 1435), are outside the scope of the National Gallery exhibition.

Recent findings suggest that some of the portraits have reverse imagery of fictive marble, and the museum is placing them in cases so visitors can view both sides. “We’re really excited to be able to show people how amazing the reverse is,” notes Nicholas Flory, who is curating the show along with Emma Capron, the museum’s curator of early Netherlandish and German painting. Flory says the elaborate reverses suggest that “these objects were not designed for a single kind of specific space or to be flat against the wall”, but rather “to be interacted with”.

Newness abounds in the show. The Arnolfini Portrait had long had an ornate Gothic Revival frame until it was replaced in 2024 by a 15th-century gilded frame. Meanwhile, the Berlin work, showing its male figure in distinctive red chaperon headgear, completed a conservation treatment in 2023 that removed distorting yellow varnish. The result of that treatment, indicates Stephan Kemperdick, the curator of Netherlandish paintings before 1600 at the Gemäldegalerie, has been to “make the palette cooler”. Before, he says, the chaperon was “fire-engine red”, and the man’s face looked “suntanned”, whereas now, he says, the face is “pinkish or whiteish—a feature that distinguished people from the better classes in the 15th century”.

Recent findings suggest that the London exhibition, which Kemperdick calls a “once-in-a-lifetime” event, is a culmination of sorts. Several Van Eyck works, including the Ghent Altarpiece, have undergone recent treatments, which Flory says has been “an impetus in Van Eyck scholarship”, and the National Gallery show reflects newly introduced research into Van Eyck’s technique, his original frames and inscriptions. Recent analysis of the National Gallery’s self-portrait, examined during its recent treatment, revealed how Van Eyck modulated the blueness of the background in the lower-right corner to “throw the sitter’s shoulder forward”, Flory says, creating a 3D effect.

Industry observers note that just out of view of the show itself, lurking in Kemperdick’s catalogue essay, is a possible bombshell: that the couple shown in the Arnolfini Portrait are not the titular Italian merchant and his wife at all, but rather Van Eyck and his wife. This would also mean that the Gemäldegalerie’s Portrait of a Man (Giovanni Arnolfini?) is also a self-portrait.

It has been revealed that the Arnolfini Portrait is among the gallery’s most popular works, and the minuscule size of the show is in marked contrast with the likely museumgoer interest. However, Flory says the diminutive roster is, in fact, the significant attraction.

“There was the possibility to expand it beyond Van Eyck and show his work in the context of his contemporaries,” Flory states. “But because he is such a monumental figure in the history of Western painting, and his portraits are so special, we really wanted to focus the exhibition on just Van Eyck himself.” Luckily, he adds, the remarkable loans, which have involved several museums sending some of their most precious works, mean “we got everything we were hoping for”.

• Jan van Eyck: The Portraits, National Gallery, London, 21 November-11 April 2027.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Marburger Farm and Ethan Good Photography.

Texas-based antique and design show Marburger Farm has unveiled an exhibition building made partly from salvaged materials sourced directly from across the 43-acre property, as shown in this video produced by Dezeen.

Called Gage Hall, the building’s facade is made from reclaimed timber sourced from around the farm and is topped with a traditional Texas metal roof and contemporary skylight elements that bring natural light into the hall.

The hall brings an additional 7,500 square feet of shopping space to Marburger Farm, bringing the fair’s total space to 100,000 square feet. Designed to honour the site’s dairy farm heritage, the hall also showcases its vision for the future.

The antique and design show has become a destination for international designers looking to source unique interior objects including furniture, lighting and vintage textiles.

The 43-acre show is located in Round Top, Texas, and has attracted designers such as Kelly Wearstler and Leanne Ford.

The fair offers visitors access to objects from over 200 independent dealers and has become one of the largest antique shows in the United States.

The site also includes a Texas-style town square, 10 restored historic buildings, four tents and a 150-year-old saloon, which has been restored to its original use as a social space and bar.

Founded in 1997, the show has grown to attract over 30,000 people annually.

The antique show takes place in January, March and October each year.

Marburger Farm is owned by Brook Partners, a Dallas-based investment tech giant focusing on culture and commerce.

It has been revealed that the company also runs the upcoming Dallas Art Fair, which is held from 15 to 18 April 2027 in Dallas, Texas. To learn more, visit the Marburger Farm website.

According to recent reports, marburger Farm Antique Show took place from 27 to 31 October in Round Top, Texas. The winter show will take place 21-24 January and the spring show will take place 23-27 March 2027. See Dezeen Events Guide for an up-to-date list of architecture and design events taking place around the world.

British Museum and Victoria and Albert Museum extend loan of Asante regalia to the Manhyia Palace Museum in Ghana

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that asante regalia gold objects on loan from the British Museum and Victoria and Albert Museum (V&A) will remain on show in Kumasi, Ghana until 2030 following the extension of loan agreements by the two UK museums. The British Museum has loaned 15 objects while the V&A lent 17 pieces, almost all of which were looted during military operations in the late 19th century.

The British Museum and the V&A signed a loan agreement in 2024 with Otumfuo Osei Tutu II, the 16th Asantehene (King of the Asante), to return the gold regalia to the Manhyia Palace Museum in Kumasi, the historic capital of what was then the Asante (Ashanti) empire. The loans will be renewed for a further three years at the end of the current term in April 2027. The two UK museums are legally unable to deaccession so the objects are being returned as long-term loans.

“The rollover of the loan agreement was always likely and from both the British Museum’s and Manhyia Palace Museum’s point of view, this has been a successful partnership with increased visitors, training and expansion at Manhyia. There is nonetheless enduring frustration from many in Ghana, both in Asante and beyond, that this is only a loan,” says Barnaby Phillips, author of The African Kingdom of Gold: Britain and the Asante Treasure.

The loan renewal announcement followed a recent visit to Kumasi by Nicholas Cullinan, the director of the British Museum, following an invitation by the Asantehene.

The gold regalia associated with the Asante royal court is on display in the Manhyia Palace Museum's Homecoming exhibition. Items shown include a small gold ornament in the form of a lute-harp (sankuo), one of the cast gold objects presented in 1817 to British diplomat Thomas Bowdich during his trip to Kumasi.

Recent findings suggest that “The British Museum has about 220 pieces of Asante gold regalia and the Manhyia Palace Museum has been involved in the selection of objects [for loan]. There has been considerable input regarding what goes back to Ghana,” adds Phillips.

The idea of a loans deal, first discussed in the 1970s, was revived when the Asantehene visited London in May 2023 to attend the coronation of King Charles III.

#33829. Gen Z apps inform approachable wayfinding for V&A East Storehouse

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (768 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dezeen ↗ Open Full Page

Gen Z apps inform approachable wayfinding for V&A East Storehouse

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (768 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • On a mission to draw in museum sceptics, Hackney design studio Fieldwork Facility looked to an unexpected source of inspiration when creating the Dezeen Award-shortlisted wayfinding for London’s V&A East Storehouse.
  • The landmark museum, completed by Diller Scofidio + Renfro last May, has been lauded for opening up the V&A‘s storage vault, including 250,000 historic art, craft and design objects, to the public for the first time.
  • The challenge for Fieldwork Facility was to help visitors navigate and interpret this trove of artefacts – especially a younger, more diverse crowd who might normally feel excluded from museums.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On a mission to draw in museum sceptics, Hackney design studio Fieldwork Facility looked to an unexpected source of inspiration when creating the Dezeen Award-shortlisted wayfinding for London’s V&A East Storehouse.

The landmark museum, completed by Diller Scofidio + Renfro last May, has been lauded for opening up the V&A‘s storage vault, including 250,000 historic art, craft and design objects, to the public for the first time.

The challenge for Fieldwork Facility was to help visitors navigate and interpret this trove of artefacts – especially a younger, more diverse crowd who might normally feel excluded from museums.

To speak to this demographic, studio founder Robin Howie decided to borrow a visual language they’re already intimately familiar with.

“We studied popular Gen-Z apps and services to understand how to make Storehouse feel intuitive as soon as you walk through the door,” Howie told Dezeen.

“Cultural institutions can all too often feel like exclusive environments with many barriers to entry. It’s unfortunately far too easy for so many people to walk into a museum, gallery or national organisation and feel a queasy sense of ‘this isn’t really for me’.”.

As an antidote, Howie and his team decided to treat the wayfinding design like an operating system in itself, looking to the UX of much-used apps like TikTok to inform signage and interaction points across the museum.

From the get-go, visitors are welcomed with an “onboarding text” that introduces them to the Storehouse and how to navigate it.

“It’s a moment that purposefully feels like opening an app for the first time where you are given a quick orientation of the experience held inside,” said Howie.

The text combines a range of different media, including printed typography, ticker tape screens and recycled paper tiles.

Topped with recycled plastic letterforms, these tiles provide a first introduction to three key colours used to mark different areas across the building.

Yellow points out viewing galleries, green is for the museum’s viewable restoration labs and pink for the Study Centre, which gives the public unprecedented access to the collection through the V&A’s Order an Object programme – a service traditionally reserved for researchers and academics.

Set into aluminium cases, these recycled paper tiles were used to form adaptable, modular signage across the building. Much like a Scrabble tile, each is emblazoned with a single letter, allowing museum staff to adapt the wayfinding based on what objects are at the moment on view.

“Storehouse’s signage system looks and feels programmable in an analogue way,” said Howie.

To suit the use across separate tiles, Fieldwork Facility commissioned a bespoke version of the V&A’s brand typeface Spiller that is monospaced.

This technique, normally used for typesetting computer code, involves shaping each letter so it occupies the same amount of horizontal space.

“The resulting Spiller Mono helps give V&A East its own unique language that is atypical for a museum,” Howie said.

“We also love that monospace typefaces were widely used in early computers and are still standard for writing and editing code – great nod to the ‘building as software’ concept.”.

On some signs, a colourful, enamelled lava-stone disc provides colour coding, echoing the yellow, green and pink first introduced in the onboarding text.

Several other interventions were also designed to encourage interaction, either from visitors or from staff, who engage with the building both as a museum and an active storehouse.

Industry observers note that to provide museumgoers with context and explanation about the pieces on show, Fieldwork Facility created interpretation labels that exist as a modular kit of components, allowing them to be fixed to Storehouse’s standardised crates, palettes and forklift-accessible shelving. Digital templates allow staff to amend these labels without relying on the designers.

The design studio even introduced dedicated “expression points” where visitors can share their opinion with the V&A staff or take part in public polls using a voting coin system.

“The operating system approach welcomes everyone to explore, define their own experience, make connections and have agency within a national institution,” Howie said.

All of the museum’s signage was designed to be adapted and reused to cut out waste, with icons for permanent fixtures – such as toilets, elevators and floor numbers – screen printed or painted directly onto the walls instead of relying on disposable vinyl decals.

Fieldwork Facility’s graphics for V&A Storehouse East have been shortlisted for graphic design of the year at the 2026 Dezeen Awards. It is up against seven other projects, including the visual identity for Dorte Mandrup’s Arctic whale watching facility and ink-free tea packaging for a Song Dynasty-themed restaurant in Guangzhou.

Industry News: ‘It is an unusual model, but I am an unusual person’: Shafeena Yusuff Ali on her Abu Dhabi foundation and gallery

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (842 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If the art world is an orchestra of players, Shafeena Yusuff Ali is attempting a one-woman band.
  • In a recent development, it was upon acquiring work for her family’s London hotel that Yusuff Ali began envisioning a career within art.
  • Vivek Vilasini’s Housing Dreams (Walls) (2014).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If the art world is an orchestra of players, Shafeena Yusuff Ali is attempting a one-woman band. Born in Abu Dhabi to the Keralan billionaire M.A. Yusuff Ali, whose Indian-Emirati conglomerate LuLu Group spans retail, hospitality and real estate, she considers among her roles: collector, dealer, art historian, writer, entrepreneur and adviser to corporate and private collections.

In a recent development, it was upon acquiring work for her family’s London hotel that Yusuff Ali began envisioning a career within art. A trio of successive master’s degrees in art history, business administration and social impact led her to establish Rizq Art Initiative in 2023, an Abu Dhabi-based organisation that includes a commercial gallery, an artist and curator residency, an education platform, an off-site exhibitions programme and an advisory. The organisation is presently in the process of separating into a for-profit commercial gallery and a non-profit foundation.

Vivek Vilasini’s Housing Dreams (Walls) (2014). Yusuff Ali has acquired a large number of works by the Indian artist Courtesy Rizq Art Initiative.

“It is an unusual model, but I think I am an unusual person,” she notes. “Notmany gallerists have three postgraduate degrees, and carry both business and academic backgrounds. I understand how industries work and I have also written an art historical paper on each work in my collection”.

Rizq, which in Arabic means “provision” or “sustenance”, was established to kickstart a nascent scene by plugging overlooked gaps in the local art ecosystem. “The biggest challenge facing the Abu Dhabi art scene is a lack of nuanced peripheral actors,” Yusuff Ali says. “Critics, fabricators, experimental spaces, warehousing and storage. For an art ecosystem to work you need all these elements to work in coherence.”.

Sources indicate that informed by Yusuff Ali’s ties to both India and the UAE, Rizq focuses on artists from the Global South, including young Emiratis Shamsa Almansoori and Reem Al Mubarak, and the Keralan watercolourist Anupama Alias Ani. Of just five commercial galleries in Abu Dhabi “we are the only one focusing on artists from the global majority”, she claims.“This is notable in a city where most inhabitants are from regions the art world doesn’t necessarily cater to.” During Frieze Abu Dhabi (18-22 November), the gallery is staging a solo show by Al Mubarak.

Beyond its Abu Dhabi gallery, Rizq also programmes offsite exhibitions, including a satellite show for the sixth edition of the Kochi Biennale in Kerala, contributing to a growing dialogue between the art worlds of South Asia and the Gulf.

Yussuf Ali's heritage also informs what she buys: areas of interest include lesser-known South Asian Modernists, such as the Keralan painter K.C.S. Paniker, as well as pioneering artists of the UAE like Hassan Sharif. Perhaps the artist whose work she has collected most widely is Vivek Vilasini, the only Indian member of the Flying House, a 2000s experimental art collective in Dubai that has hugely influenced today’s contemporary art scene in the UAE. “Vivek is a friend,” Yusuff Ali says. “It is remarkable that an Indian artist in the UAE has played such a central role in defining the nation’s art history.”.

As for Abu Dhabi, Yusuff Ali believes in the long term, and understands that the local market is “only just beginning to grow”. Presently her private funds keep Rizq’s gallery afloat, but she is quick to point out that she speaks the language of business alongside art. “I have established a proof of concept and spent the past three years demonstrating measurable impact,” she tells The Art Newspaper. “I am confident that the next time we speak, we will have brought enough patrons on board to become profitable.”.

The Art Newspaper: What was the first work you bought?

Shafeena Yusuff Ali: The first significant work was a Mona Saudi sculpture, Mother and Child (1981), before she passed away. I bought it when I was pregnant—and at a generationally different price. When I was buying it I fully realised it was special.

It has been revealed that A painting by one of the forgotten masters of Kerala, N.K.P. Muthukoya.

If you could own any work from a museum what would it be?

I’d like to hang a work by Amrita Sher-Gil alongside one by Princess Fahrelnissa Zeid. My life bridges South Asia and the Middle East and these two women are strikingly similar in how they lived painful but luxurious lives.

Where do you like to eat in Abu Dhabi?

My favorite shawarma place is Al Akkawi.

What do you recommend doing outside the fair?

It has been revealed that november is perfect biking weather. Walk around the city—don’t drive. And get a boat to one of the outer islands. They can be really magical.

What is your least favourite thing about art fairs?

Sometimes it gets too homogenous—the same seven galleries showing the same seven artists.

What should people know before coming to Frieze Abu Dhabi?

The culture here is quite shy, and highly relationship based. Newcomers might struggle if they lack patience.

• Frieze Abu Dhabi, Manarat Al Saadiyat, 19-22 November.

Film and photography by Jim Stephenson.

The restoration of an art deco pavilion and lido near MacDuff, Aberdeenshire, shortlisted for the RIAS Andrew Doolan Best Building in Scotland Award, features in this video by photographer Jim Stephenson.

The film is the latest in a series being published by Dezeen in collaboration with the Royal Incorporation of Architects in Scotland (RIAS) to highlight the annual award’s 2026 shortlist.

In the video, viewers are shown the Tarlair Outdoor Pool Pavilion, revived by London-based Studio Octopi to bring its tea pavilion and pools fully back into use.

The studio aimed to retain the historic character of the 1930s art deco building, while introducing considered upgrades, including a marble-clad exterior.

“We wanted to pay homage to the art deco period, which the building was originally conceived in,” said Studio Octopi director James Lowe.

“The green came about really in connection with the paint samples that we took off the railings, and it was decided to go with marble that would give resilience to the environment.”.

Established in 2002, the Andrew Doolan Best Building in Scotland Award is an annual award that highlights Scottish projects, with this year’s winner set to be revealed on 26 November.

Comprising three reuse projects, RIAS stated this year’s shortlisted projects tap into “notable conversations around community, collaboration, retrofit and reuse”. Shortlisted alongside the Tarlair Outdoor Pool Pavilion is the Paisley Central Library by Collective Architecture and the Edinburgh Futures Institute by Bennetts Associates.

Last year’s winner was a public park renewed by studios Stallan-Brand and LDA Design.

The film and photography are courtesy of Jim Stephenson.

The Lumix SHX1 Box-Style Cinema Camera Is The Spirit of Varicam Reborn

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, panasonic has announced the Lumix SHX1, the first compact cinema camera to bear the Lumix branding.
  • “For decades, Panasonic has supported the video industry from broadcast to cinema, and its Varicam cinema cameras have been used to make films, dramas and documentaries worldwide.
  • Sources indicate that “In 2024, Panasonic took this further by integrating its professional AV and consumer imaging businesses, which share a commitment to supporting customers’ creativity.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, panasonic has announced the Lumix SHX1, the first compact cinema camera to bear the Lumix branding. Previously, Panasonic separated its cinema and consumer imaging divisions between the two brands, but the SHX1 is the unification of the two under one roof.

“For decades, Panasonic has supported the video industry from broadcast to cinema, and its Varicam cinema cameras have been used to make films, dramas and documentaries worldwide. This expertise has also been carried into Lumix, and it led to the Lumix S1H, introduced in 2019 as a cinema-quality professional video model,” Panasonic notes.

Sources indicate that “In 2024, Panasonic took this further by integrating its professional AV and consumer imaging businesses, which share a commitment to supporting customers’ creativity. The new Lumix SHX1 brings together the expertise of both businesses in a compact cinema camera.”.

The combination of the two Panasonic camera divisions and the existence of the SHX1 effectively means the end of the Varicam brand, but should result in a more cohesive overall camera line.

According to recent reports, the SHX1 is, effectively, the S1 II packed into a box-style cinema body, with a couple of exceptions. Firstly, Lumix included an anti-aliasing filter to reduce moire at the cost of some sharpness while the camera also offers the ability to shoot BRAW, albeit with a caveat: it can’t capture it to the CFexpress or SD card slot and must instead use an external SSD.

Beyond that, the camera is capable of capturing basically what the S1 II already does. It features a 6K full-frame partially stacked CMOS image sensor with Dual Native ISO and Dynamic Range Boost, giving the camera effectively 15 stops of dynamic range when in V-log. The SHX1 comes with ARRI LogC3 pre-installed as well, allowing users to choose between V-Log and ARRI LogC3.

Recent findings suggest that in standard recording formats, the camera supports 6Kp30 and 5.1Kp60 in 4:2:0 10-bit, as well as in 3.8Kp48 4:2:2 10-bit, which is a new option compared to the S1 II. It also, of course, supports open gate recording and in-camera anamorphic de-squeeze.

The sensor is equipped with a Phase Hybrid autofocus system with 779 points and the SHX1 has the same AI technology as found in the S1 II which enables eye and face detection. Also on-board is Panasonic Lumix's excellent five-axis in-body image stabilization system along with support for Dual IS 2 when combined with a lens that supports OIS and the feature.

Recent findings suggest that professional interfaces include 12G-SDI and HDMI output, timecode input/output, and internal 32-bit float audio recording through the 3.5mm microphone input. The thermal design supports unlimited recording time in up to 4Kp120 and the design of the box camera means it supports micro V-mount batteries, too. Of note, there is no in-camera ND filter, which is an odd exclusion given the target market.

Panasonic also announced two optional accessories: the XLR Handle Unit AU-XHU1 and the Control Grip AU-GRP1.

The Panasonic Lumix SHX1 is slated to become available in January 2027 for $4,699.99. A kit that includes both the handle and the control grip will be avaialble for $5,499.99.

Shure’s New MV360 Mics Promise to Make Spatial Audio Capture Easier

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (517 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Petapixel

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Shure is entering the increasingly crowded spatial audio market with its new MV360 microphones.
  • Just last week, Blackmagic Design unveiled the Ambisonic Microphone, a high-end studio solution.
  • Shure states its newly introduced MV360 “makes immersive audio more accessible to creators at every level.” To achieve this, the plug-and-play mic features ready-to-use Capture Modes, including immersive binaural, stereo, mono, and auto-tracking.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Shure is entering the increasingly crowded spatial audio market with its new MV360 microphones.

Just last week, Blackmagic Design unveiled the Ambisonic Microphone, a high-end studio solution. Last month, Sony arrived on the scene with its ECM-AX10, a $250 spatial audio mic for content creators. Built with creators in mind, Shure’s upcoming $349 USB-C MV360 is much closer to Sony’s offering in both price and functionality.

Shure states its newly introduced MV360 “makes immersive audio more accessible to creators at every level.” To achieve this, the plug-and-play mic features ready-to-use Capture Modes, including immersive binaural, stereo, mono, and auto-tracking.

Recent findings suggest that the mono and stereo modes are self-explanatory, working just as they would on a traditional mic. Immersive binaural promises a broader, more lifelike soundstage, which Shure states is ideal for headphone playback. Meanwhile, auto-tracking mode focuses the virtual microphone toward the loudest sound source, such as a speaker in an interview or podcast.

According to recent reports, each Capture Mode records a ready-to-use two-channel file that requires no post-production. However, creators who opt for full 360-degree recording gain significantly more flexibility, as they can edit the Ambisonic B-format (Ambix) file in Shure’s Motiv software or compatible third-party apps.

As Shure explains, the MV360 captures a stronger sense of place than a traditional microphone.

“Listeners can feel closer to a podcast conversation, more immersed in an ASMR scene, or transported into the middle of a bustling market or quiet forest,” Shure claims.

Industry observers note that the MV360 is a relatively compact spatial microphone housed in an all-metal body. It records and draws power over a single USB-C cable, ensuring compatibility with a wide range of devices, including smartphones and many cameras. Alongside Shure’s Motiv apps, the MV360 supports various third-party applications, allowing owners to record 360-degree audio directly to Motiv or a DAW of their choice.

“Sound can make the difference between watching a moment and feeling part of it,” notes Eduardo Valdes, Associate Vice President of Global Marketing and Product Management at Shure.

“Until now, capturing that sense of presence has required expensive equipment, technical expertise and time that many creators simply don’t have. The MV360 changes that. It gives creators an easy way to bring listeners closer to the conversation, the performance or the world around them, while giving experienced professionals the control they need to shape every detail,” Valdes continues.

The Shure MV360 is available now for $349 and includes the USB-C mic, a small tripod, cold shoe mic clip, phone clamp, extra cables, carrying case, and windscreen.

Recent findings suggest that alongside the standard model, Shure also unveiled the MV360+ today, slated to arrive in early 2027. Designed for field recordists, videographers, and VR storytellers, the MV360+ works with mirrorless cameras, DSLRs, action cameras, 360-degree cameras, and more. It also adds onboard 32-bit float and internal recording capabilities, a rechargeable battery, and wireless control functionality.

The Shure MV360+ will retail for $449 when it arrives early next year.

Latest Update: Panasonic Lumix SHX1 Review: The S1 II in Boxy Clothes

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1401 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Petapixel

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that when the Panasonic S1 II was announced, one of my first thoughts was, “How are they going to top this with an S1H II?” The answer was, they didn’t.
  • If the box-camera form factor is a benefit for the work you do, the SHX1 is one of the best.
  • Note that throughout this review I will be referring to this camera in comparison to the Panasonic S1 II.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that when the Panasonic S1 II was announced, one of my first thoughts was, “How are they going to top this with an S1H II?” The answer was, they didn’t. Instead, Panasonic is bringing the internals of the S1 II to a newly introduced form factor, a cinema box camera, and calling it the SHX1 ($4,699).If the box-camera form factor is a benefit for the work you do, the SHX1 is one of the best. However, for content creators, it offers only minor upgrades over the less expensive and still incredibly capable S1 II. ProsClass leading image stabilization never seen in this style of cameraFantastic image quality with minimal rolling shutterExtremely modifiable designConsNo internal BRAW (requires an SSD)Some buttons feel mushy and are difficult to pressNo internal ND filter This is definitely not the FX5 competitor many were waiting for, but it still might make a lot of cinematographers and videographers very happy.

If the box-camera form factor is a benefit for the work you do, the SHX1 is one of the best. However, for content creators, it offers only minor upgrades over the less expensive and still incredibly capable S1 II.

Note that throughout this review I will be referring to this camera in comparison to the Panasonic S1 II. If you are unfamiliar with that camera, you can check out our review here. As well, as the SHX1 does not offer any stills capture, this review will be entirely focused on video capture.

Sources indicate that the SHX1 is quite compact for a cinema camera, similar to a RED Komodo and weighing only 948 grams (33.4 ounces). In a departure from Panasonic’s previous BG-Series box cameras, this SHX1 includes a top-mounted LCD monitor, with extensive 4-axis articulation and 1.84M dots of resolution.

According to recent reports, the articulation is extremely useful, as you can shoot above your eye-line, something usually prohibited with top-mounted displays. There are dedicated exposure buttons on the body, as well as Menu, Back and AF-On. These buttons have a pretty unresponsive feel to them, with little haptic feedback to let you know you’ve actually pushed the button. These can be customized, something I recommend to avoid excessive menu diving.

As expected for a cinema camera, the top, right side and bottom of the camera have plentiful 1/4-inch mounting points for rigs and accessories. The camera is powered by Mini V-Mount batteries, most of which are the same height as the camera. There is an active fan system in the body, which allows even 4K/120p footage to be captured indefinitely.

It’s worth pointing out that you can also purchase the SHX1 with an accessory kit ($5,499), which includes a top handle, XLR adapter and a side grip. The grip feels fantastic but is quite large. I consider it almost a necessary accessory, and the extra controls give operators several more options for custom buttons and a joystick for selecting the autofocus point. The top handle is very sturdy, and the removable XLR adapter gives you easily accessed gain controls. Unlike previous S-Series bodies, which relied on an XLR adapter to capture 32-bit float audio, the SHX1 can record 32-bit audio through the 3.5mm jacks and internal mic as well.

Footage can be stored on a UHS-II SD card, CFexpress Type B card, or external SSD. As expected with a cinema camera, there are locking ports for SDI video, timecode, and a full-size HDMI port. For further external control, a Live Production Unit called the AU-LPU1 will be released in early 2027.

It has been revealed that the lack of built-in ND filters is a disappointment, but that was the compromise Panasonic was forced into when keeping the body so small. Screw-in filters or a matte box will be required for controlling light levels.

The sensor is the same full-frame 24.5MP partially stacked unit we saw in the S1 II, which is capable of outstanding results and well-controlled rolling shutter. The only difference is an anti-aliasing filter has been added to minimize incidents of moiré in finely detailed textures.

In my testing, though, I found very similar results to the S1 II, with neither camera giving me moiré even when shooting fabrics at moderate distance.

Like the S1 II, the SHX1 has a massive number of recording resolutions, frame shapes and frame rates. The headline feature is 6K Open Gate recording up to 30P, and 5.1K Open Gate using the full sensor up to 60P. For slow motion, the camera can capture 4K at up to 120P with sound. There is also the option to expand the dynamic range by reducing the readout speed. This does produce appreciably cleaner shadows, but with a corresponding increase in rolling shutter artifacts.

Video can be recorded with MP4, MOV and ProRes codecs for standard 10-bit video. There is also the option to capture 12-bit RAW video in either ProRes RAW or BRAW flavours. Bafflingly, though only ProRes RAW can be recorded to the CFexpress card, BRAW requires an external SSD. This is particularly odd as BRAW offers extremely efficient 12:1 compression rates, which could be easily written to a card. Adding insult to injury, the camera’s startup time is dramatically increased with an SSD attached, taking nearly 10 seconds and often leading to me missing shots.

According to recent reports, the video quality itself from the camera is outstanding, with impressive detail and expansive dynamic range even when Dynamic Range Boost is not active. Log video can be captured in either Panasonic V-Log gamma or ARRI’s LogC3. The Panasonic V-Log gamma remains my favourite log curve to work with, but ARRI’s gamma is very flexible and the industry standard in the filmmaking world.

What sets the video quality from the SHX1 apart from any other box camera is the inclusion of incredibly effective in-body image stabilization, based on the S1 II system. This works great in its default mode, but even better when Panasonic lenses are attached and the “Cropless” stabilization is engaged. The camera’s autofocus abilities are also quite reliable, though perhaps not quite as rock-solid as Sony’s and Canon’s more recent implementations. Humans and animals can be automatically detected, and there is a good degree of “stickiness” when following moving subjects.

If you don’t require the box-camera form factor, then the SHX1 can be a confusing proposition. The S1 II features nearly all of the video capabilities with excellent photography specs and an EVF in a considerably more affordable package.

However, many professional videographers and cinematographers require the box-camera design to make it easy to build rigs or mount the camera in a variety of locations. The forthcoming Live Production Unit will add further versatility for using the SHX1 as a remote camera, something the S1 II cannot offer.

As well, if absolute reliability is important, the more robust cooling system in the SHX1 means overheating will not be a concern even when recording demanding footage in hot areas. The S1 II has very good thermals for a hybrid mirrorless camera, but in professional situations absolute reliability is imperative.

According to recent reports, compact cinema cameras like the RED Komodo-X 6K ($4,995) and Blackmagic Pyxis 6K ($2,249) offer similar form factors and outstanding image quality. Unlike the SHX1, these can record extremely compressed RAW video internally. However, the autofocus performance is vastly behind the SHX1, and neither offers IBIS. RED and Blackmagic may offer more bang for the buck for filmmakers, but the SHX1 is the clear choice for handheld documentary work.

RED Komodo-X 6KBuy newly introduced on B&HRED Komodo-X 6KBuy used on KEH.comBlackmagic Pyxis 6KBuy new on B&HBlackmagic Pyxis 6KBuy used on KEH.com.

It has been revealed that the Sony FX5 is also a compact full-frame cinema camera with great autofocus and IBIS. The FX5 can accept an optional EVF, has more reliable autofocus and records compressed X-OCN RAW video internally. However, the SHX1 features much more effective stabilization and industry-standard connections. For event work, the Sony makes more sense, whereas the Panasonic will find itself more at home in commercial environments.

Maybe. If the box-camera form factor is a benefit for the work you do, the SHX1 is one of the best. However, for content creators, it offers only minor upgrades over the less expensive and still incredibly capable S1 II.

Xiaomi’s Eye-Catching Pro Series Phones Go Global for the First Time

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1329 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Petapixel

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Xiaomi officially released its 18 Pro Series phones, the 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max, at a launch event in Paris, marking the first time it’s pushing its Pro models outside of China.
  • It has been revealed that update 11/17: An earlier version of this story incorrectly stated that Pro mode did not support 50-megapixel RAW image capture.
  • Both will hit select markets — not North America — in the coming weeks and months and carry on Xiaomi’s existing partnership with Leica as camera-centric devices.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Xiaomi officially released its 18 Pro Series phones, the 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max, at a launch event in Paris, marking the first time it’s pushing its Pro models outside of China. That also makes them outliers in another respect: they are rare slab smartphones with two displays.

It has been revealed that update 11/17: An earlier version of this story incorrectly stated that Pro mode did not support 50-megapixel RAW image capture. It is supported on the Xiaomi 18 Pro Max.

Both will hit select markets — not North America — in the coming weeks and months and carry on Xiaomi’s existing partnership with Leica as camera-centric devices. They also feature a rear LTPO AMOLED screen positioned as a creative tool for those who like selfies but want more variety.

Xiaomi already foreshadowed this launch when unveiling the devices at Qualcomm’s Snapdragon Summit in September 2026, so specs, especially on the camera side, weren’t entirely a mystery. Once they released in China shortly afterward, the cat was pretty much out of the bag.

Sources indicate that we know the main differences between the two phones have to do with screen size, image sensors, the Snapdragon chip, and battery capacity. The 18 Pro Max gets a larger 6.9-inch LTPO AMOLED display (2624 x 1208) with Xiaomi’s own Shield Glass protection, a 1-120Hz variable refresh rate, 4,000 nits of peak brightness, and BT.2020 support. It also runs on the more powerful Snapdragon 8 Gen 6 Elite Extreme chipset and packs a 7,050mAh battery.

It has been revealed that otherwise, the Pro has a smaller 6.4-inch panel (2436 x 1120) with the same display specs as its Max sibling. It also steps down a bit, running on the Snapdragon 8 Gen 6 Elite chip, and, given its smaller size, has a 6,000mAh battery.

Recent findings suggest that xiaomi first showcased its Privacy Display feature for the main screen on both phones when it launched these devices in China, and it works the same on either model. When activated through the settings, it recommends eight applicable apps, including Notes, Gallery, Messages, Google Photos, Gmail, Phone, and Contacts. Consumers can also enable it for any installed app via the Privacy Display settings, or choose to leave the feature on at all times, regardless of what’s onscreen.

There are slight differences in the rear display size, as the 18 Pro Max features a larger 2.9-inch panel compared to the 2.7-inch screen on the 18 Pro. Both will come with 12GB of RAM and 256GB or 512GB storage configurations, though the Pro Max also offers a 16GB RAM and 1TB storage variant.

Industry observers note that interestingly, Xiaomi equips both phones with almost the exact same camera specs. The three Leica-branded rear cameras are largely identical on both models, with one key exception: the 18 Pro Max uses the LOFIC-equipped Light Fusion 960L sensor, whereas the 18 Pro uses the standard Light Fusion 960.

It has been revealed that the 200-megapixel main camera (23mm equivalent) uses a Type 1/1.28 Light Fusion 960L image sensor and an f/1.67 aperture. Thanks to LOFIC technology, it delivers better dynamic range than both a standard sensor and the 18 Pro’s main camera. You can tell just by pointing both phones at any subject before even snapping the shutter. There’s also optical image stabilization with a CIPA-rated seven stops of shake correction. The Leica Summilux-designed lenses combine precision glass and plastic elements with what appears to be a glare-resistant coating.

In a recent development, the 200-megapixel periscope telephoto camera (75mm equivalent) uses a Type 1/1.56 image sensor, an f/2.4 aperture, and 3.2x optical zoom. Finally, there’s the 50-megapixel ultra-wide camera, whose sensor size remains a mystery. It is somewhat of an outlier in that it’s a 17mm equivalent with a 102° field of view, which is noticeably narrower than most ultra-wide cameras on other phones.

On the software side, Xiaomi adds a new mode called Essential Moment that marries Leica color science with AI-driven image processing to emulate classic film and camera looks. Names like “B&W Film,” “Modern Vintage,” and “Iconic CCD” don’t specify exactly what stock they’re based on, but the new styles add a distinctly Xiaomi-infused element to the camera interface.

This is how Xiaomi frames it: “B&W Film captures the depth and tonal range of classic monochrome photography, Iconic CCD recreates the vivid, saturated colors of CCD-era digital cameras, and Modern Vintage offers refined tones with natural detail for a timeless look. Consumers can also replicate the optical characteristics of two classic lenses — a 35mm Documentary lens and a 75mm Portrait lens with soft bokeh.”.

There are some unusual limitations, however. There is still no 24fps option for video, including in Pro Video. None of the Leica styles and filters introduced in the Leitzphone by Xiaomi have migrated over to these devices, so you retain the same choices offered in other Xiaomi models. Further, while the Pro Max can capture 50-megapixel RAW photos in Pro mode, the standard Pro model cannot.

The Back Display offers a fairly high degree of access to the overall camera interface, including modes, settings, customizations, and more. Xiaomi limits zoom to 0.7x and 1x, meaning there is no way to activate the telephoto camera, though the settings still let you hold up a palm to trigger the shutter hands-free.

While the live preview occupies a sizable portion of the display, Xiaomi configured it to light up in bright white elsewhere to help illuminate subjects in dimmer conditions. It limits available modes to Photo, Video, Portrait, and a retro-style option called Photo Booth, and strangely omits Leica filters from the equation (though you can still choose between Leica Authentic and Vibrant as the overarching style).

In a recent development, you also get the choice to shoot pixel-binned 12.5-megapixel or 50-megapixel stills, with video resolution options ranging from 720p all the way to 8K at either 30 or 60fps. Dolby Vision and a Teleprompter are also available as optional features.

It’s a fully functional display in that it works with swipes and gestures just as the main display does. Tap-to-focus works, as does focus tracking when double-tapping on yourself or another subject in the frame. You can preview shots you’ve taken and either press the onscreen shutter or use the volume buttons to capture a photo or video.

Since the screen uses the rear cameras, the dynamic range advantages apply equally; Xiaomi doesn’t appear to neuter the experience by dialing things back, particularly with the LOFIC sensor on the 18 Pro Max.

In a recent development, an added benefit of the Back Display is that it also works with notifications and real-time information, like calls, maps, ride-hailing, food delivery, audio recording, and more. Pin to Back Display allows you to pin text and images to it for quick reference, such as a boarding pass or QR code. There’s also the option to apply a different wallpaper to it, if you want.

Recent findings suggest that neither Xiaomi nor Leica made any mention of a photography or teleconverter lens kit for either phone, even as Xiaomi’s Chinese competitors continue to release more of them. There are possibilities there, but you would need a third-party setup to make it work. Thus far, Xiaomi has only made photography kits for its Ultra line, which it maintains is still the company’s flagship with a more specialized photography slant.

You won’t find the Xiaomi 18 Pro or 18 Pro Max in Canada or the U.S. unless you import them yourself. They’re both compatible with North American cellular networks, so there isn’t a hardware limitation in that regard. Warranty challenges aside, Xiaomi is offering five years of Android updates and six years of security updates.

Industry observers note that both models will come in the same four color variants: Black, White, Velvet Red, and Cosmic Blue. As for pricing, the Xiaomi 18 Pro starts at €1,399, while the 18 Pro Max starts at €1,599.
